speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition) moved:
speechtext: For a copy of all orders in council passed since the 23rd day of October, 1935, excepting appendices and treasury board minutes and excepting orders already tabled.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say to my right hon. friend that I am pleased to see him back in the house. I hope he has quite recovered from his slight indisposition of last week.
I wish I could agree to the motion he is asking to have accepted by the house. I submit however that it is a motion without precedent. As far as I can discover nothing of the kind has at any time been granted by any parliament of the British empire. The motion is for copies of all orders in council passed since the 23rd day of October, 1935. That is to say, it is a request for blanket authority to obtain all orders in council passed within the past six months, or, in other words, since the present administration assumed office. It does not specify the particular subject or subjects in relation to which my right hon. friend desires to have information. It makes no reference to any particular class of orders, it is simply an unlimited request for all orders in council that have been passed. As hon. members well know, there are orders in council and orders in council. There are some
which arise as matters of routine; there are others which relate to more important matters. To fill an order of this kind would involve considerable expense and a very great deal of labour on the part of the public service.	,
I hope my right hon. friend will be able to tell us his reasons for asking for this. It does seem to me an unreasonable request to make. I have asked the clerk of the privy council whether he is aware of anything of the kind ever having been granted at any time. He informs me that, of his knowledge and of the officers of the department, no such request, if it has been made, has ever been, granted. What my right hon. friend is asking now would establish a precedent which might, be a very serious one if it were followed on subsequent occasions. For example, there is no reason why some hon. member should not immediately give notice of a motion for copies of all orders in council passed while my right hon. friend was in office. That would be equivalent to the request the right hon. gentleman is making now, his request covers all orders in council passed by the present government up to the present time.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I have sought, by glancing at authorities on parliamentary procedure and practice, to discover anything which would throw light on the attitude to be adopted by the house towards a request of this kind. The fact that there appears to be no mention of anything of the kind by any authority I have been able to consult thus far, would indicate that nothing of the kind has ever been contemplated by writers on matters of parliamentary practice and procedure. I do find, however, the following *reference in Todd's Parliamentary Government in England, volume I, page 440:
Considerations of public policy, and a due regard to the interests of the state, occasionally demand, however, that information sought for by members of the legislature should be withheld, at the discretion and upon the general responsibility of ministers. This principle is systematically recognized in all parliamentary transactions: were it otherwise, it would be impossible to carry on the government with safety and honour. Whenever it is declared, by the responsible servants of the crown, that any information sought for in parliament could not be supplied without inconvenience to the public service, or for other sufficient reasons, the house refrains from insisting upon its production.
My right hon. friend will see at once that, if his request were granted, it would mean some minister of the crown would have to go over all the orders in council to see if, perchance, there was any single order, in the collection asked for by the right hon. gentleman, which it might not be in the public
Motions for Papers

interest to lay on the table of the house. I do say to the right hon. gentleman that I think his request goes too far. I remember that some years ago Sir Henry Drayton, then leader of the opposition, made a motion very similar to that which my right hon. friend is now proposing. It was for a return of all orders in council passed in the calendar year 1925. I shall read the answer I then made on behalf of the government:
I would ask my hon. friend if he really desires all that he is requesting here. As my hon, friend knows, there are a great many orders in council that are purely routine orders, having to do with regulations, promotions, transfers of land, property and so forth, and to bring down all that is asked for here I am afraid would mean a very large and quite unnecessary expense. If my hon. friend would indicate the orders he has in mind there would be no objection.
My answer to my right hon. friend's request to-day is just the same as that given to Sir Henry Drayton ten years ago. If my right hon. friend has any particular orders or class of orders in mind which he would like to have, the government will be only too ready to consider his request. I hope however he will not press a motion which is in the nature of seeking to obtain from this house a general warrant to search the files of the privy council with a view only of seeing if he cannot discover in them something which may serve for purposes of discussion later on.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: May I make a few observations, Mr. Speaker? It is a strange thing indeed if we have reached the stage in Canada where parliament cannot be made aware of the orders in council passed by the executive.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We have not
reached that stage.

What has been said
by the right hon. gentleman is that we are not to have access to the orders in council passed since he came into power because, first, they might disclose something that should not be disclosed and, second, that considerable expense would be involved in their preparation.
As to the second point I took the trouble, I think it was in the month of November, to telephone the clerk of the privy council that probably I would make such an application to parliament, and I suggested that he prepare an extra copy of the orders in (Council when he was having them prepared. J think he accepted that suggestion in the spirit in which it was made; at least I asked

him if he had done so and he told me he had prepared them but that in some cases further copies had been asked for and there were some he would have to prepare over again.
Let us look at this thing fairly. I have no desire to press unduly for information to which I am not entitled, but for five long years we were charged with governing Canada by order in council. On every platform in the country we were charged with governing Canada by order in council. I now propose to ask that parliament be shown the orders in council that have been passed since October 23 last, to see the extent to which it was necessary for the executive to use its powers for the purpose of carrying on government.
Secondly, there can be no valid order in council that has not behind it some statutory authority, except it be an order in council authorized by the prerogative of the sovereign. Eliminating consideration of the second matter, it therefore follows that any order in council that is valid, that has been passed by the governor in council, must have behind it some statutory authority. I put that to the Minister of Justice some sessions ago and he admitted it to be a correct statement of the law. It has been decided by the court of highest authority in the British realm that there must be a statutory authority for the exercise of the executive power when passing orders in council, aside from trifling exceptions which have no application here. The extent to which the government of the day have found it necessary to utilize the powers which it is said were improperly exercised by the late administration I desire to know-that is, the extent to which the powers have been exercised since October last-and the only way I know of ascertaining that is by asking for a copy of the orders in council and from such copies ascertaining the extent, to which the authority conferred upon the government by this parliament has been utilized during the past six months. It is idle to say, in fact it concedes the correctness of my position when it is said, that nothing appears in the books about it, because it is always taken for granted that you get the orders in council anyway. This is the first time I have ever heard the suggestion that the House of Commons is not entitled to every order in council that is passed. There is nothing in the books for the simple and obvious reason that it is taken as a matter of course. In many cases it is provided that the orders in council shall be printed in the Canada Gazette. For instance, those which have to do with the authority conferred upon the executive under

Motions for Papers
peace, order and good government have to be published in the Gazette. A synopsis or precis of relief orders in council also has to be published in the Gazette, and when the house is in session they have to be tabled. That is why the motion reads "excepting orders already tabled."
But the final argument used by the right hon. gentleman himself is conclusive of the soundness of my request. He said: If you will indicate what orders in council you want, then of course the government will be happy to produce them. Suppose I divide my request and say I will make four or more applications: one, all under the Relief Act; two, all under the authority of the Department of National Defence; three, all under the Department of Agriculture; four, all under the Department of National Revenue; five, all under the Department of Railways and Canals and Marine; six, all under the Department of Public Works; seven, all under the Department of Justice, and so on. Now the right hon. gentleman says: That will be quite all right. I have specified what I want. But because I add them all together and say I want them all, the Prime Minister says that is an improper request and one he hopes I will not press. All I can say is that I regret to inform the house that I had a very definite purpose in putting this notice of motion on the order paper. I desire these orders in council for very many purposes, all of which I do not propose at the moment to communicate to the house, and I am greatly surprised that the right hon. gentleman should have taken the position that I am not entitled to them. I am not asking for them for myself; I am asking that they be brought down as a return so that we may ascertain to what extent the government has been conducted by the executive under the authority of statutes heretofore passed, or, if any, under the prerogative powers of the sovereign.
I have no desire to add to the amount of work to be done, and that is the reason I took the step I did early in the fall, to obviate unnecessary expense. I do not ask it as any personal accommodation at all, but in the exercise of my undoubted parliamentary right I have asked that a return be made to this house of the evidence of the exercise of its authority by the executive, in order that we may be able to see for ourselves what it discloses.
I desire to thank the right hon. gentleman for his kind reference to my health, and I greatly regret that after his courteous and friendly reference to myself I cannot accommodate him to the extent he has suggested.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The motion is of course not debatable, but perhaps the house will grant me the permission to say just a word in reply to my right hon. friend. He has spoken of "the correctness of the position"-I think he used that phrase-in asking for the production of documents in the House of Commons. I must say I was amazed when I heard my right hon. friend state that he had given directions to the clerk of the privy council-
No, I did not say "directions," I was very careful in that regard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What did my right hon. friend say?

I said I had telephoned to the clerk of the privy council intimating that I proposed to make such an application to the house and that he should keep that in mind when preparing his documents as it might save some expense.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The request thus made by my right hon. friend involved making additional copies of public documents, thereby adding to the expense of the records of the privy council. If he had wished anything of the kind he is an old enough parliamentarian to know that his communication should have been addressed to the president of the privy council wTho is the minister responsible, and not to the clerk of the privy council. My right hon. friend would have taken very strong exception if, when I was leader of the opposition, I had telephoned to the deputy ministers of the different departments and told them what I expected them to have ready when I came to speak in the House of Commons, especially when the matter involved public expense, and would involve, on the part of the deputy, either the embarrassment of bringing the matter to the attention of his chief or of being silent in the matter and seeking to meet the wishes of the leader of the opposition rather than of the ministry itself.
However, the motion involves a very important question of procedure, and I still take the position that this house cannot be expected to grant a general warrant for the production of all orders in council which may be passed. My right hon. friend, I am sure, must have been familiar with my reply to Sir Henry Drayton made ten years ago, to which I referred this afternoon-
No, I had not seen it, I was not in the house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I take- my right hon. friend's word for that. However,

Privileges and Elections
I do not think he is surprised that, in view of the responsibility I have with respect to the production of public documents, I do not accede to a request which involves creating a precedent as far-reaching as the one he proposes. May I say to my right hon. friend that, if he will indicate the particular subjects on which he wishes to get information, the government naturally will take his request under consideration and accept the responsibility for either refusing or granting it. We are anxious to accommodate him whenever it is in order so to do with the fullest information possible in regard to all proceedings of the government. But I must respectfully decline to grant the present request, which is in the nature of a resolution for omnibus authority to obtain access to pretty much everything which has been done by the privy council, since the present government came into power, and is of record in the offices of the privy council.

The government have been passing them every day this session.
Motion negatived.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATUS OP SPEAKER OP COMMONS BETWEEN DISSOLUTION AND NEW PARLIAMENT-PROCEDURE WITH RESPECT TO RETENTION OR DISMISSAL OF EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two matters to which I wish to direct the attention of the house in dealing with this resolution. First, it is the custom in the mother of

parliaments when a question of privilege is discussed to have the Prime Minister a member of the committee. For the time being he is supposed to have a greater interest than anybody else in the maintenance of the privileges of parliament, because he has control of the government of the day. It will be recalled perhaps by hon. members that when Mr. Churchill in the British house made a statement regarding the attitude taken by the Lancashire board of trade-at the instance, it was said, of Lord Derby-a committee was set up and Mr. MacDonald in fact presided over the deliberations of the committee on privileges in which the matter was investigated. That is the first question. I am not quite sure whether the Prime Minister is a member of the committee on privileges and elections.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATUS OP SPEAKER OP COMMONS BETWEEN DISSOLUTION AND NEW PARLIAMENT-PROCEDURE WITH RESPECT TO RETENTION OR DISMISSAL OF EMPLOYEES
speechtext: No.

subtopic: STATUS OP SPEAKER OP COMMONS BETWEEN DISSOLUTION AND NEW PARLIAMENT-PROCEDURE WITH RESPECT TO RETENTION OR DISMISSAL OF EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
At any rate, it is a large committee. Usually matters of this kind are set down for a committee on privileges smaller in number than the one we have here.
The second question is as to whether or not the motion is sufficiently comprehensive to permit an investigation regarding the dismissal of employees in the early part of this year, and the employment on a tentative basis of their successors. As I read the motion it is probably broad enough for that purpose. I have no objection to offer to the resolution; for I had proposed when the committee was organized to ask that it consider the matter, and I have taken certain preliminary steps for the purpose of getting information to enable me to do so, subject to what I have said as to whether or not the motion is sufficient. I take it that it is sufficient to enable all questions of that kind to be gone into. I see no objection to the matter being considered, remembering however that we have a statute which the committee cannot construe, but which must be interpreted ultimately by a court of law. Presumably some of those who were dismissed this spring will bring action against the Speaker to ascertain whether or not he had any such power as that which was exercised. That is a matter of interpretation of the statute, and one with which the committee cannot possibly deal.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATUS OP SPEAKER OP COMMONS BETWEEN DISSOLUTION AND NEW PARLIAMENT-PROCEDURE WITH RESPECT TO RETENTION OR DISMISSAL OF EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
I thank my right hon. friend for suggesting that I should be a member of the committee on privileges and elections. It is a standing committee of the house, and I notice in looking over past records my right hon. friend, while Prime

European Situation
Minister,, was not on that committee. I imagined I would be following a precedent which would appeal to him as a good one if I followed his example in not placing myself on the committee at the time it was constituted. If there should be something in what my right hon. friend has said as to the desirability of the Prime Minister being on the committee, in the event of some situation arising in the committee which might materially affect matters of procedure or authority with respect to the House of Commons I shall be glad to hold myself in readiness and, if the committee so desire later on become a member of it. However I have no doubt that in so far as I am able to limit the number of obligations I have to meet each day it will the better serve the interests of all others concerned, as well as my own interests.
As to my right hon. friend's observations to the effect that he is not sure whether the motion is broad enough to cover all points he may have in mind, or those which other hon. members may have in mind, I would direct the right hon. gentleman's attention to what I said on February 13, when I was giving the house an assurance as to the desire of the administration to make the reference as broad as might be desired by all parties. I am reported at page 179 of unrevised Hansard as follows:
If the reference is not broad enough when it is submitted by the administration, and if it appeals to the house as being desirable to make it any broader. I give every assurance that the desires of the house will be acceded to.
I doubt if it is possible to go farther than that.

subtopic: STATUS OP SPEAKER OP COMMONS BETWEEN DISSOLUTION AND NEW PARLIAMENT-PROCEDURE WITH RESPECT TO RETENTION OR DISMISSAL OF EMPLOYEES
speechtext: I think that is right. May I say a word in explanation of what I meant when I made the suggestion as to the Prime Minister being a member of the committee. The Prime Minister's duties are so onerous that ordinarily his being a member of the committee on privileges and elections would be out of the question, but when there is involved a point respecting the power and usages of the House of Commons itself, with relation to the Speaker and employees of the house, I think a distinction must be made. I believe it was in consequence of that view that Mr. MacDonald presided over the special committee on privileges which dealt with the case of Mr. Churchill. That action was taken because it was considered a matter of great importance to the house itself.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour) :	Mr. Speaker, this matter had

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sent a note
to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) indicating that when the orders of the day were called I would ask if he had any statement to make regarding the European situation. While I am on my feet may I say I think the Prime Minister is entirely right when he says I should have telephoned him, not the clerk of the privy council, with respect to the matter under discussion a few moments ago. speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as he has
just said, my right hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) was kind enough to send me a communication indicating that on the orders of the day he would ask whether the government might, wish to say something with regard to the present European situation. The fact that he
European Situation

communicated with me gave me an opportunity to examine the .procedure followed in the British House of Commons in regard to this very matter. Had he not given me notice I might not have had the opportunity so to do.
I believe I could not answer my right hon. friend better than by quoting from the statement made by the Foreign Secretary, Mr. Anthony Eden, in the House of Commons at Westminster on the 20th instant, that is to say on Friday of last week. The Hon. Mr. Eden said:
I must first thank all parties in this house for the forbearance they have shown since I last made a statement here, March 9. This forbearance, I can assure the members of the bouse, has been a real help to us in our negotiations and in the work upon which we have been engaged.
I recognize further that this willingness to refrain from pressing the representatives of the government for information, during admittedly very difficult negotiations, has not lessened the anxiety with which the whole house views the present situation and it is for that reason that I am taking the first opportunity to give the house as much information as I can.
I would point out that our house has all the information which it was thought advisable by the Foreign Secretary, speaking at Westminster, to be given the British house on the 20th instant. I question if there is anything we of this house could add which would be helpful to those who at the moment are involved in very critical and delicate negotiations on a matter of supreme concern to mankind. I hope, and I am sure, hon. members will feel that an attitude on their part similar to that which has governed in the British house towards the administration in requesting a statement is one which they will be prepared to take. The government has been kept informed by dispatches of the general trend of negotiations. I am not disclosing any fact which I should not disclose when I say that what has subsequently appeared in the public press has very closely parallelled the information which we have received. Here and there, there may have been some statements given to the government which have not been given to the public, but generally speaking the information we have received is very similar to that which has appeared in the public press and has been received at about the same time as it has appeared in the press.
I did point out, speaking in this house a few days ago, that Canada was not a party to the Locarno agreement, and that the negotiations arise out of the Locarno agreement. There has been no question, I think, on the

part of anyone as to the statement I made in that particular being a perfectly accurate statement of our position. In the circumstances I think it would be in every way preferable, having regard to the extremely critical nature of the negotiations and the fact that the situation keeps changing not only from day to day but sometimes from hour to hour, for hon. members of this house to forbear, if they can see their way so to do, from preferring any request which might provoke discussion in our country at this time.

If I may say so, I think the statement made by the right hon. gentleman has answered the very questions I had in mind. It was asserted that we were not being kept informed; that appeared recently in one of the newspapers. The right hon. gentleman has answered it and made it perfectly clear, first, that the government has been kept informed by the government of Great Britain as to what has been going on, and secondly, that, qua Locarno itself, this government was not a party to that treaty. The third matter has only been touched upon, and that, is the question of the position of Canada in the negotiations. I think perhaps the right hon. gentleman is quite correct when he says that that is covered by what he has already said, to the extent to which it goes; and it is certainly not my purpose, nor would it be the purpose of anyone associated with me, to precipitate a debate that might in any way lessen or limit or imperil the powers which the British authorities are exercising in their effort to bring about world peace in the face of very grave difficulties.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
May I say that while we
appreciate what the Prime Minister has said with regard to the information that is being furnished by Great Britain to this government and to the public, the Prime Minister has not indicated in any way whatever what the attitude of this government is under the circumstances. It is quite true that we are not a party to the Locarno treaty, but we are a member of the League of Nations, and, as I understand it, the recent action of Germany is an infringement of the covenant. What is the attitude of Canada, or have we expressed an attitude either to Great Britain or to the league with regard to what we consider that action of Germany might involve? It seems to me that we cannot go on indefinitely without having some indication from the government as to what the attitude of Canada is.

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I say to
my hon. friend that, in a word, the attitude of the government is to do nothing itself and if possible to prevent anything occurring which will precipitate one additional factor into the all important discussions which are now taking place in Europe. I believe that Canada's first duty to the league and to the British empire, with respect to all the great issues that come up, is, if possible, to keep this country united. I believe that can be more effectively accomplished at this stage if we wait until we are a little more fully informed, than we are at the moment, with respect to all the considerations of which we should have knowledge before attempting to pronounce too definitely upon the position which we are taking or shall take with regard to European affairs.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As I was leaving my office I learned that a dispatch had come from London with respect to the naval treaty to which the hon. gentleman has referred. It had just been deciphered, and I have not thus far had an opportunity of acquainting myself with the particulars of it.
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 13, respecting a certain trade agreement between Canada and the United States of America.

I
shall be very brief, but on the second reading of this bill I desire to put on record one or two matters. During the progress of the schedules through the committee information was sought from time to time with respect to exports from and imports into the United States since the treaty came into operation. These figures were not available. I have now before me figures issued by the United States department, as published in the New York Times, and I think they should be drawn to the attention of the house.
Though the total exports of the United States to all countries of the world for January were valued at $197,958,000 as compared with exports by them in December of $223,555,000, or a decrease in total exports of approximately $26,000,000, at the same time the United States exports to Canada in January, after this trade agreement came into operation, greatly increased in dollar value as compared with December, 1935. In January, 1936, the exports from the United States to Canada amounted to $26,990,000, and in December, 1935, their exports to Canada amounted to $21,760,000. The United States exports to Canada in the first month of the operation of this treaty showed an increase of $5,230,000 over the previous month. Canada's exports to the United States for the same period should likewise be interesting, as we are supposed to have obtained such material benefit under this agreement. In. the month of December, 1935, Canada's exports to the United States were valued at $26,937,000, in round figures, but for January, 1936, they were valued at only $22,934,000, a decrease of $4,003,000.

On section 3-Orders in council authorized.

This section provides an excellent illustration of the necessity of the executive having power to deal with questions which prior to 1930 it was said should be considered by parliament. The section reads:
The governor in council may, notwithstanding the provisions of any law in force in Canada, make such orders and regulations and do such acts and things as are deemed necessary to carry out the provisions and intent of the said trade agreement.
Any other law may be overridden by regulations having to do with the well being of

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
this treaty. This is another illustration of the necessity of having these powers vested in the executive. This section is exactly the same provision as will be found in all treaties that have been ratified by this house. When I was in another place the right hon. gentleman, in the days when he was in office, used this section as we are using it to-day, but there was much criticism and complaint. In my judgment this section is being very properly used, because otherwise it would be impossible in some cases to carry out the treaty itself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Since my right hon. friend approves of my actions, I have nothing further to say.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word about this section of the bill. I speak for what I think I can fairly say is a typical industrial riding, the city of London. In order to lay the basis for that claim, I should like to detail briefly some of the manufactured products made, in my riding, most of which I feel will be very seriously affected by this section in particular and by the agreement in general. In the city of London we have two large steel plants. We have one of the largest establishments in the dominion turning out brassware, plumbing specialties, water softeners and so on. We have a cereal factory and four large hosiery mills. We have two boot and shoe factories % and one of the largest tanneries in Canada, and I believe the oldest. We have a large biscuit factory, a hat and cap factory and three large plants turning out paper and cardboard boxes and containers. We have one of the largest creameries in the dominion and four printing and lithographing plants. In addition, there are manufactured in London on an extensive scale electric refrigerators, radios, chemical products, agricultural implements, concrete mixing machinery, vulcanizing equipment, radiators, barrels and barrel staves, metal garages, metal doors and hardware specialties, soap and cleansing materials, poultry and stock feeds, poultry and stock remedies, chewing gum and candy. We also have a large iron moulding concern, and we have two large and excellent breweries. I do not think that any hon. member can seriously contest the statement that I speak for a very representative cross section of Canadian industrial life.
I do not agree with the remarks made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) when he was replying to the speech of my right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett) during the course of the debate on the resolution leading up to this bill. The minister is quoted on page 720 of Hansard as follows:

then I come to the effect on our factories. Meu are being released from employment, my right hon. friend says, in some of those branch factories to-day because it is cheaper to produce the goods in the central United States. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have made some inquiries. Some of the very few branch factories from which men are being released are branches of United States concerns which have been in existence m Canada in recent years with extremely high protection, achieved by means of arbitrary valuations, which had no economic justification for existence.
Taking my own riding as a criterion, I should like to say that the condition of affairs of which my right hon. leader complained is not confined to a very few factories. This condition is affecting very many factories and very many Canadian work people of both sexes. If what has occurred in the past month or two goes on progressively, it will be a matter of great seriousness to every artisan in this dominion. The minister then went on to say that these factories and the arbitrary valuations have no economic justification. I should like to invite the minister to my riding and have him extend the few inquiries which he says he has made. This condition is one of such tremendous importance to the country that it should not be dealt with on the strength of a few inquiries by anybody. I think I can promise the minister that if he will come to London and extend those few inquiries he will find that in that city, at all events, whatever he finds in the rest of the dominion, what I have said is perfectly true. I suggest that when he is there he interview some of my constituents and explain to them, in his convincing and charming way, that these factories which have given them employment at good wages during the past four years, and the arbitrary valuations which have made it possible for those factories to operate, have no economic justification whatever. If the minister is successful in convincing one single worker who has lost his or her employment as a result of the operation of the agreement now under consideration, and as a result of the reversal of the tariff policies of the past four years, I shall certainly be the first one to congratulate him heartily.
Speaking primarily for industry, I am unalterably opposed to this agreement, because I cannot see anything in it other than an increase in unemployment. To my way of thinking it is bound to have this result, by crippling industries already in operation in this country and by preventing the setting up of new ones. I will give two illustrations from plants in my own riding. One is the largest of its kind west of Toronto. During 1935 thirty per cent of that plant's total production consisted of items manufactured on

Canada-V. S. Trade Agreement
a royalty basis under licence from American concerns which could not get their goods intc this country because of the tariff policies ol the previous government, and which manufactured them through this company in London and in so doing enabled it to profit by the arrangement and to give employment tc a great many workmen and workwomen in London. This factory has already suffered from the effects of the present agreement, and there is no doubt that as time goes on it will suffer considerably more.
Let me take another example of the manner in which the tariff policies of the previous government have helped industry in my riding. There is another plant engaged in an entirely different line of products. It is the Canadian home of an American concern manufacturing the world's most popular breakfast food. Until the advent of the empire trade agreements the plant in question manufactured in London purely for domestic consumption. Following the passage of the empire trade agreements it started exporting to empire countries, and during most of the year 1935 it exported to those countries at the rate of 170 railway cars a month. Between 1932 and 1935 the company greatly increased the area of its plant by building an addition to it, and also more than doubled the number of its employees. I mention that in connection with this section 3 simply because I see in the present Canada-United States agreement a real obstacle to the continuance of the empire trade agreements, a threat to the success which we have enjoyed under those agreements, and a handicap in re-negotiating them in 1937. And while the empire trade agreements are being mentioned, I must deplore the diatribes that we have heard from the opposite side of the house since the house has been in session, and from supporters of the Liberal party in the course of the election, directed against the empire trade agreements on the ground that they were engendering an unfriendly attitude towards Canada on the part of the people of England. I submit that the evidence is all to the contrary, and I would refer to a debate that took place in the parliament at Westminster after the empire trade agreements had been in force for two years. The government which negotiated those agreements for the United Kingdom was returned to power in the fall of 1934 with a very substantial majority.

Up to the present I have not interrupted my hon. friend, because, as he is a new member, I
did not like to raise a point of order which might perhaps affect what he has to say. I cannot see, however, that his remarks are relevant to the section we are discussing. The house having approved sections 1 and 2, is now dealing with the question of orders in council authorized, to which the hon. gentleman's leader has referred. What he is now saying in discussing the empire trade agreements is, it seems to me, quite beside the point.

May I submit as to the point of order that I have made the statement that this agreement we are considering is going to make the renewal of the empire trade agreements extremely difficult, and therefore anything I say in support of the empire trade agreements and against allegations made against them should, I submit, be in order.

I listened very carefully to the remarks of the hon. gentleman; I did not interrupt him, realizing that he is a new member, but this matter should not have been discussed under section 3, because section 3 deals specifically with orders in council.

May I suggest,
Mr. Chairman, that you passed section 2 very quickly? I was not at all sure that it had been passed; he intended to speak on that section.
