speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not wish to preclude my hon. friend. Let him proceed.

When this new parliament
assembled, with its fresh mandate, in the course of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne a Liberal amendment was introduced to the address in substantially these terms:
Resolved that the policy of the government is not conducive to the restoration of imperial and world trade.
That amendment was debated very fully on both sides, and in the course of the debate many very bitter attacks were made upon the empire trade agreements, in very much the terms, I may say, that we have heard in this house in the course of this session. When the vote was taken the amendment was defeated by 358 to 25. To put a fine point to the story the only people who supported the amendment were twenty-five Liberals of the Manchester school. The remainder of the house voted against it. the score being about fourteen to one. I submit to you, sir, that what the English people think about these trade agreements can be gathered better from their House of Commons-a very representative house if there ever was one, because I would remind you, Mr. Chairman, that there was a very large percentage of labour votes in those 358 votes -than from what is said by, let us say, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) who made the statement that an unfriendly attitude was being engendered in England by these empire trade agreements.
Then let us bring the story down a little more to date. Within the past month, or to be exact five weeks, the British high commissioner, Sir Francis Floud, addressed a very large gathering at Hamilton on trade matters, and in the course of his remarks he spoke in an extremely kind way of these empire trade agreements. I remember that one statement he made was that thanks to these empire trade agreements and the export of apples to the United Kingdom resulting therefrom the standard of the British product had gone up. Surely if there is an unfriendly attitude towards these trade agreements in England their high commissioner would not come out here and speak kindly of them at a public gathering. It is true that at the same meeting Sir

Francis Floud urged on his audience that they buy more British goods, but that is what he is here for, and I sincerely hope the Hon. Vincent Massey is saying the same things to the audiences of England. The mere fact that Sir Francis Floud urges us to buy more British goods cannot possibly be construed as an indication of an unfriendly attitude towards these trade agreements.
Then, Mr. Chairman, let us bring this inquiry right down to date. I hold in my hand a copy of the United States weekly newspaper Time, of March 16. On page 23 I find this very interesting item:
The United Kingdom's motor industry is acutely sensitive to Canadian competition, has not hesitated to sneer in paid advertisements at "the American cars which are so conveniently brought in from Canada" under empire tariff agreements. At great advertising expense a feeling has been nurtured in the United Kingdom that to buy a Canadian car from beyond the seas is not really to "buy British."
The article goes on:
This notion was blasted and a page of empire business history turned ...
Than the article describes how last week a closed car was ordered from Oshawa, Ontario, for the use of a very great personage indeed, one who has been referred to as the best business man in the British empire, whose name I am not allowed to mention in this house but whom you, Mr. Chairman, will readily recognize. My submission is that if the gentleman to whom I refer buys a car from Canada-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Order.

-a car which he is enabled or tempted to purchase by virtue of these trade agreements, surely we have the most convincing evidence available that there is no feeling of hostility towards these agreements in England.
I quite realize, sir, that if we are to do our duty in this parliament we must legislate not for one section of the country or for one group of its workers; we must legislate for the dominion as a whole. I fully appreciate that in any comprehensive trade agreement with the United States certain interests must suffer, and as the representative of an industrial riding I was quite prepared to take with good grace certain minor sacrifices provided the compensation received by the country as a whole was adequate. But having sat in this chamber for the past month and having heard the various schedules discussed in detail I am forced to say that in my opinion this is an extremely lopsided agreement. I find scattered throughout the schedules, dotted here and there amongst the concessions given us, quotas

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
that to a very large extent destroy the utility of those concessions, and I find what appear to me to be extraordinary anomalies. As an example I find that the truck farmers, the vegetable growers of our country, who already struggle under a very severe climatic handicap, are now in the unfortunate position that most of the commodities they produce come into this country at lower rates than are granted their products entering the United States. It seems to me that there is no possible justification for anything of that sort. Then I go further; I look to the east and I find our fishermen dealt with in a very grudging way. It seems to me there has been nothing more than a gesture made to help the fishermen of the maritime provinces. I know there is a good deal of feeling along those lines in the maritimes and I cannot help wondering how it was that so many Liberal maritime members failed to record their votes on the resolution leading up to the introduction of this bill. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that there is some significance in that state of affairs.
I should like to ask the hon. member how many maritime members did not record their votes.

I think possibly my hon. friend, as a maritime member, is in a better position to answer that question than I am; I simply say that many of them did not vote.
I should like to point out, pursuing what I was saying previously, that any adverse effect on one section of our community or on one particular class of workers is going to be felt right through our whole national life. My submission is that the effects of this trade agreement are going to work in a vicious and ever widening circle. To-day the industrial worker will suffer, to-morrow the farmer whose best customer the industrial worker has been will suffer, and the day after that the railway man who moves the products of both these classes will suffer.
In conclusion let me say that I am not opposed to the principle of trade with the United States. I do feel, however, that if we run the risk that a comprehensive trade agreement with a country twelve times our own size entails we should do it only if we are adequately compensated for the very real risk that attaches to such an experiment. I put it to you, sir, in the form of a homely illustration. I suggest to you that if you were attending one of the large enthusiastic political picnics that the good people of Rimouski stage in your honour from time to time, and the hour for sports had arrived and you saw one little fellow tying himself
up for the three-legged race with a man twelve times his size, you would be struck by the sight. Then if when the race started this ill-assorted couple were to pull into the lead, you would be tempted to remark: Why, that is a smart little fellow! But suppose a follower of this sport who was at your elbow said: Oh, I don't know about that, because those two have run together before. You might inquire how they made out, and suppose he were to say: They did all right for a while, but that big fellow has a nasty habit just when things are going best of pulling a knife out of bis pocket and, without any reason, cutting the ties that bind them, whereupon the little fellow falls down on the track and everyone tramples on him; you would be tempted to remark, "Oh, oh!" or words to that effect. And suppose it were carried a step further and your friend said: Furthermore, there is another big fellow, much bigger than that big chap there, who wants to run with the little fellow, who has-been running with him for the past four years; they have been keeping perfect step, they have been away in the lead, but now the little man is turning him down for this other fellow. I am sure you would say the little man was crazy. My submission is that in entering into this trade agreement for the very inadequate benefits we receive we are acting in a most ill advised way. Therefore I propose to vote against this section and against the bill and to work against it in this house and out of the house, and I say that in the fulness of time-and it may not be very long-my party will be supported in the action we are taking on this measure.

Mr. Chairman, I was most interested in what the hon. member for London (Mr. Betts) has just said. He spoke about Rimouski; he knows the lower St. Lawrence because I know he spent his summers when he was younger on the north shore of the lower St. Lawrence, though it is quite a distance from Rimouski. The hon. member spoke about the big fellow, three times the size of the little fellow-
Twelve times.

So much the better, the big fellow being the American and the little fellow the Canadian; and he spoke of a race. But in this agreement there is no race; it is a matter of trade. And the hon. member should not forget that if the American is twelve times as big as the Canadian he requires twelve times as much clothing; he must eat twelve times as much; his shoes and socks must be twelve times as large, and even his

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
watch should be bigger-I do not see that such a big man would be contented with a small wrist watch-and so on. That is the point of view that I offer in reply to the hon. member for London.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Coming into force.

I think this section is improper as it is now drawn. This agreement has been in force since January 1. Section 4 has been copied from the section used in connection with other treaties that came into force when proclaimed. If it were not for certain features of this agreement it would not be necessary for it to come before parliament at all. The intermediate tariff may be granted to the United States without coming to parliament, as it was granted to Germany and Austria, if compensation which in the opinion of the governor in council is adequate is obtained, as the Prime Minister pointed out the other day. This agreement is now in force by reason of the action taken by the executive; the executive has reduced the duties in accordance with the provisions of the law, I take it, to the point indicated in the schedules to the agreement. The schedules became effective on January 1 last. It is also true that the United States took similar action. But here we say the act shall come into force on a day to be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council. I think probably the draftsman responsible will consider it necessary to revise this section; for it certainly would mean that since last January this agreement has not been in force, when as a matter of fact it has been. And someone will have failed in the collection of duties if it goes in its present form; for if it does not come into effect until there is proclamation, obviously between January 1 last and some time before when the orders in council were passed there has been failure on the part of someone to collect the revenues called for in the schedules. I think this section will have to be amended to provide that the act shall be deemed to have been in force since January 1, 1936.
But that is hardly correct with respect to the whole of it, because part of it is not in force yet. For instance the binding of free goods on the part of the United States on the one hand and of Canada on the other is not in my judgment a matter that could be effected by executive action. That is one of the reasons why it is necessary to come to parliament. It is equally true that there are one or two other matters that stand in

the same position, but inasmuch as the agreement has been in effect in respect to duties, it struck me, looking at it the other day, that it would have been ample to say, "this act shall come into force on the day of assent thereto." That would make it effective with respect to all matters that cannot be covered by executive action. Obviously there are several matters that executive action could not deal with, but all that executive action had power to cover it is unnecessary to say anything about, because such matters stand in the same position as, for instance, the granting of intermediate tariffs to Austria or to Germany. In connection with the French treaty and the Brazilian and the New Zealand and the Polish treaties it was provided that they should come into force on proclamation. They did not come into force until proclamation was made. As these schedules are now in force and the revenues are being collected on that basis, it seems to me that all that is necessary is to say either, "This act shall be deemed to have been in force since January 1, 1936," or, "This act shall come into force on the day of assent thereto, except so far as it is already in force by virtue of the powers exercised by the governor in council under the appropriate statutes." I think the section requires amendment in that respect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The point my right hon. friend has raised was carefully considered when the bill was drafted. It is not correct to say that the act is in force. It will not be in force until after there has been at Ottawa an exchange of the proclamation, and of the ratification of the agreement. Part of article 15 states:
The provisions of article 1 and of articles 3 and 4, respectively, shall, subject to the reservations and exceptions elsewhere provided for in this agreement, be applied by Canada and the United States of America on and after January 1, 1936, pending ratification of the agreement in respect of Canada as provided in the first paragraph of this article.
What it amounts to is that the schedules have been applied, pending the enactment of the measure itself. If the measure were not enacted there is no doubt that one country or the other would very speedily withdraw what has been granted by executive action. The one provision which will make these schedules binding until December 31, 1938, is the section the committee is now discussing, namely the one which fixes the time at which the act will come into force. I spoke of this matter when the agreement was in committee. My right hon. friend may not have noticed whait I said at that time. I assure him that

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
this phase of the enactment has been carefully considered by the law officers, and they say that the section as drafted is correct.

I have been considering the point raised by the leader of the opposition and to which the Prime Minister has spoken. Without taking up too much time in its consideration it seems to me that we might meet the situation by using the words: "This act shall come into force on a day to be fixed by proclamation by the governor in council, and when so proclaimed shall be deemed to have been in force from January 1, 1(136."
That covers it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I should like
were it advisable to do so to accept what the hon. member has suggested. I must however say to him that the very point he has raised has been considered by those who have considered the provisions of the bill from a legal point of view. The government is advised that the additional words are unnecessary, and would I believe be misleading. The provision had better be left as it is.

One always hesitates to disagree with the law officers. In fact, it is idle to disagree, because there is ample majority to see that this agreement shall become effective. But certainly we have here a self-contradictory provision-perhaps selfcontradictory is not the proper expression, but I believe it will convey the sense of what I desire to say. The right hon. gentleman has pointed out the inconsistency between the two. This is a statute; it is not an agreement. The statute ratifies and approves the agreement. It is true that there must be a formal exchange of notes at Ottawa by which the agreement is accepted by both parties. By international usage it is contemplated that the act does not come into force until after that date, whatever the date may be. This statute says, however, that "this act shall come into force on a day to be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council." We know that the agreement which is part of the act, and which must be read with it as part of it, has been in force since January 1.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, only the schedule.
But the schedule is part of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

And must be read in conjunction with and taken as part of the statute. That is, Bill No. 13, which one day will become the statute, by section 2 provides 12739-86
that the agreement set out in the schedule of the act, as it was approved, shall have the force of law notwithstanding the provisions of any other law in Canada. Since the first of January the schedule has already had the force of law in Canada because there was power under the statute so to declare. This bill states, however, that notwithstanding the provisions of any law in force in Canada this shall have the force of law, and is hereby approved. It is approved as of date to be fixed by proclamation. That is section 2. Section 4 of the bill states that the proclamation fixes the date; therefore the approval relates to the date. But it has been approved by the governor in council and there has been a reduction of duties brought about by executive action, which reductions have been operative for the last two months. By the time this bill becomes law they will have been in operation three months.
I have no desire to interpose technical difficulties, but when I was speaking the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) suggested leaving the section as it is, but adding thereto the words: "and when so proclaimed shall be deemed to have been in force from January 1, 1936." That addition preserves the point made by the right hon. gentleman, one which I quite appreciate, and also preserves some consistency with respect to the conduct of business in Canada. I suggest it would be an anomaly to say that for a period of three months both the United States and Canada have been carrying into effect the schedule of an agreement now being ratified by parliament by an act which states that it shall not come into force until the date fixed in the proclamation. It struck me that the hon. member by the suggested addition provided for that very contingency. There is the formal ratification by the two governments, then the proclamation, and then the statement in the statute whereby the proclamation is made that it shall be deemed to have been in force since the first day of January, 1936, which is absolutely in accordance with the facts.
We have acted upon the assumption, rightly or wrongly, that in our official conduct, apart altogether from questions of duties, since the first day of January the agreement was binding upon us in every particular. While I have no desire to place my views against those of the law officers of the crown I can only say that, as a matter of using the statute as an expression of the will of the house, it is the will of the house as indicated by the Prime Minister that this statute shall come into force on proclamation. But it is also the will

Canacla-U. S. Trade Agreement

of the house, because action of the executive has been approved, that this statute shall be deemed to have been in force since the first day of January of this year. If that provision were added I think the measure would not be open to any doubt as to its consistency, and there will be no anomaly, because it would then be thoroughly consistent with the whole intention of the government as expressed from time to time in the house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: May I say to my right hon. friend and to the hon. member for Leeds that the adoption of the words they have suggested, namely "shall be deemed to have been in force since the first day of January," would imply that the schedules had not been in force by virtue of statutory authority. Such is not correct. My right hon. friend will recall that while in office he was responsible for a measure which gave to the governor in council the power to lower duties against any country which might give to Canada reciprocal-
No, not reciprocal-concessions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, concessions. It was under that authority that, so far as Canada is concerned, up to the present action has been taken with respect to the schedules. That authority will continue until the act in all particulars becomes effective. There are clauses in the bill other than those relating to the schedules. If we were to adopt the words my right hon. friend has suggested we would be saying that the other sections, which it was never intended should come into effect until the act as a whole was in effect, had been in effect since January 1. That might get us into grave difficulty with respect to some action taken or which, were the act already in force, should have been taken. It would not be desirable to run a risk of that kind.
Similarly, so far as the United States are concerned the reductions which have been made by the president have been made under the authority not of this agreement but of powers given to him by congress with respect to making reciprocal agreements with other countries. That authority applies to the reduction of duties. Let me repeat to the right hon. gentleman that the reduction of duties on both sides has been effected under an authority which existed at the time negotiations respecting the agreement were entered into. These reductions are legal in all particulars; they are being carried out under the authority given by statute, but they will not continue indefinitely unless very soon an agreement is ratified which will make them

binding over the period of the next three years. It is important therefore that the act should set forth that these schedules will be binding along with the other clauses of the agreement up until the date which has been fixed for its possible termination.

I take it that the object
of this bill is to confirm, ratify and make valid in every respect the agreement that has been entered into between Canada and the United States. The Prime Minister says, and I have no doubt accurately enough, that the governor in council had authority to reduce the duties in schedule I. That may be true; but as we are confirming the agreement it seems to me, and I so submit in all sincerity, that it is well to have the ratification of the agreement in every respect and in every detail, even though the action of the governor in council may have been valid and may have authorized and did authorize the reductions made. But now we are putting on this agreement the seal of approval of parliament, and it seems to me that we ought to go all the way and make our ratification and approval complete. It puts it on a stronger legal ground and prevents any possibility of question as to the regularity of anything done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend were a member of the government responsible for the agreement I am sure he would not wish to put into the legislation approving the agreement any clause which would imply that some action taken prior to the enactment of the measure had not been wholly valid. Having had the best legal advice in this matter throughout I believe we shall be erring on the safe side if we hold to the advice on which we have acted.

I wish to correct a false
impression which may be created in the country by the hon. member for London (Mr. Betts) who spoke this afternoon. He wanted to know why so many Liberals from the maritime provinces had not voted for this agreement. I would call his attention to the fact that on the date the vote was taken the maritime provinces had twenty-five members elect, there being one vacancy. Of the twenty-five members elect there was one Conservative, the lone star from New Brunswick. The others were all Liberals from the maritime provinces, and out of those twenty-four Liberals twenty voted for the agreement. Four happened to be absent.

I have a word to say
in reply to something that has been said by one of the members representing Vancouver, who spoke about the lumber business. At

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
the time I did not have a bound set of Hansard and I used the unrevised edition. But I remember distinctly that in his speech on October 12, 1932, the then Prime Minister spoke about the lumber business. His remarks will be found in the middle of the right hand column of the page on the right hand side. He said that our previous trade with the United States in lumber-our exports-amounted to $32,000,000 and that our trade with Great Britain was some hundreds of thousands of dollars in excess of $6,000,000. That meant that our trade with Great Britain was only a small fraction of our trade with the United States. For a time our best market for lumber was England; and then our lumbermen changed it for the United States, mainly because that was nearer. I have the honour to represent a constituency which is on the border line, and therefore it is much more profitable for my constituents to trade with the United States. In that very speech on October 12, 1932, if my memory serves me rightly, the right hon. gentleman mentioned the tax which had been imposed by the United States on Canadian lumber-so much per thousand feet. That duty has been a real handicap to our people. I did not vote on the treaty because I did not want to commit myself on that before seeing the effect of it. I give the government the benefit of the doubt and I approve of the treaty because it is a gesture which shows our willingness to trade with our neighbour. This is understood by all the people who know a little about the lumber business, and that is why I insist on it. The right hon. gentleman said in the same speech that it was on account of that new duty which had been put on lumber by the United States that our exports were falling. I read that many times three years ago, and it struck me that it was the reason why the trade had decreased so much. Now it was a matter of retaliation. It is always dangerous to have a tariff contest with another country in the upper grade. The result may be most appalling in the long run. This is what happened. The tariff was raised against every country in the world. The United States retaliated to a certain extent, and now the government is showing willingness to trade with the United States. It is a very good move, for it is an incentive to better trade with all the nations of the world.

I am glad the hon. gentleman made that correction, which confirms what I have said. I am sure he remembers distinctly what he himself said, and whether you call it a revenue tax or a duty is immaterial. There was either a revenue bill or a customs bill-you may call it what you like-which imposed a certain amount that had to be paid on Canadian lumber going into the United States, and the consequence was that the yards were full of unsold lumber for many years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Before the bill is reported out of committee, if I may be permitted to express it as such, I should like to say one last word.

I take it the
schedule will have to be carried?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Section 2
reads:
The trade agreement between Canada and the United States of America set out in the schedule to this act is hereby approved and shall have the force of law notwithstanding the provisions of any law in force in Canada.
I believe the adoption of that ' section carries with it the schedule referred to therein. I do hope it will not be found necessary again to run through the three weeks' discussion we have already had on the schedules.

It is usual in
committee for the chairman to say, "Shall the schedule carry?" I suppose we could deal with the schedule as a whole.
The carrying of section 2 does not carry the schedule; it is put to the committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not going to deprive hon. gentlemen opposite of the opportunity of reopening the schedules if they so desire and in due course the chairman will call them.
During the course of the last month we have been discussing this agreement almost every day the house has been sitting, and I do not think there is any doubt left in the minds of any one as to where in the main difference lies between hon. gentlemen opposite and those who support the agreement. As the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has said, time alone can show whether the agreement will be one of mutual advantage to the two countries or whether it will reveal the fact that one country has secured much the worse or much the better of the other. I am afraid that short of the period of the agreement the difference

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
of view between us will hardly be reconciled. Admitting, however, the difference of view, we ent-ertain as to the merits of the agreement. I hope that from now on all parties will find it possible to accept the agreement in the spirit which was expressed so admirably by one who was a former leader of the Conservative party in Canada and a former prime minister, a gentleman whose name is greatly honoured by hon. members opposite and greatly respected by all parties. Speaking on January 30 to a meeting of the shareholders of the Crown Life Insurance Company, of which he is president, Sir Robert Borden is reported as follows in referring to the new trade agreement:
Reviewing, in brief, conditions as they exist in Canada to-day, Sir Robert pointed out that abnormal unemployment, the railway situation and high taxation still confront us, and must not be unduly minimized, and that international intercourse is still hindered by instability of exchange and high tariffs.
"On the other hand," he pointed out to the well-attended meeting, "the recent arrangement for reduction of tariffs and wider trade between Canada and' the United States, apart from any question as to relative advantage which remains to be determined by events, has given an inspiring lead which may be followed elsewhere."
I submit that Sir Robert, being no longer in the active arena of party controversy and being able to take a detached view of the matter, may be regarded as being in a position to express an opinion which I believe will be found to be largely that of independent minded persons of this country. I believe that if this agreement is accepted as something which gives a lead in connection with trade intercourse between nations, at a time when a lead is greatly needed we shall find as the years go by that it has proved to be of great advantage, not only to the two countries that are parties to it, but to other countries of the world as well.

Mr. Chairman, I had
intended to make a few observations on the third reading of this bill, but they can be made very satisfactorily at this time. The remarks of the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden were not directed to an approval of this bill or of this agreement. He said that freer trade relations between the two countries were desirable, but he has not expressed the idea nearly as strongly as we endeavoured to express it in November, 1934, nor any stronger than I endeavoured to express it on two occasions in London, speaking for the government of the day. The bill now before the committee contemplates two things. First of all, it contemplates an agreement with the United States of America. That in turn involves the consideration of two questions, with

one of which we are wholly in accord and with the other of which we are not in accord.
As to whether it is desirable to have freer trade relations with the United States, we are all agreed. We have said that and have repeated it. We have been assailed for making that statement, it being said that .*e did not mean it. Notwithstanding what was said the other day by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), during my lifetime I have never known the time when the Conservative party did not hold to that point of view. Ever since 1878, when Sir John Macdonald enunciated the national policy, the position of the Conservative party has been perfectly clear on that point.
We come now to the second question, the terms of the agreement. It is upon this question that the whole argument turns; there the right hon. gentleman and I are in complete accord. He says that he and his supporters regard the terms of the agreement as satisfactory; we have voted in this House of Commons to record that we do not regard these terms as satisfactory. We do not believe that they give opportunity for a single day's work to a single Canadian. We do not believe that they present an opportunity to diminish the number of unemployed in this country by one. This matter has engaged the attention of hon. members for several weeks. They have considered it from many angles and the more it has been dealt with, the more I think it has been apparent that while this or that item may be desirable from a Canadian standpoint, taken as a whole the agreement is not beneficial to the people of Canada. The right hon. gentleman has very properly said that the ultimate determination of that issue must await the passing of time and the performance of the agreement in the years to come.
Briefly, what is the position? First, the power to make this agreement has been challenged in the United States. It is contended there that there is no power in the president to exercise the authority which he did in making this agreement. It has been said that the power to make an agreement of this kind rests with congress and it being a trade agreement, the senate of the United States must approve by a two-thirds vote. That is a question with which we have nothing to do; it must be settled and determined by the people of the United States and their supreme court. I noticed the other day that the question is now up for litigation although only a very small sum of money is involved. The issue has been .presented to a federal judge for consideration, but that issue we may leave outside the question altogether.

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
Let us ask ourselves half a dozen questions and then I shall have concluded. First, what have been the benefits to agriculture? What have been the benefits to wheat, oats, barley and rye? Has any one of these commodities in which we are so greatly interested been given wider markets in the United States of America by virtue of this agreement? The answer is no. There has been no lessening of the barriers imposed to enable these commodities to reach the markets of the United States. What about potatoes? With respect to seed potatoes there are some benefits although there are quota limitations, but with respect to the great mass of potatoes produced in this country, can it be said that there has been a widening of the market in the United States for Canadian potatoes? On the contrary, as the matter stands to-day, not only may potatoes come into Canada more freely than they did, but they are in fact coming from Michigan and from Maine, into the markets of New Brunswick and of Montreal, and into the markets of Ontario at Windsor and Toronto; they now have access to our markets on more favourable terms than ever before.
Then, let us go to the dairy products: butter, eggs, cream, milk, and what do we find? Under the tariff that prevailed against this country prior to the late government coming into office, the tariff preceding the Hawley-Smoot tariff, agriculture in Canada was crippled, but those duties are exceeded by the duties which now apply to Canadian products. Cream, which carried a duty of twenty cents prior to 1930, now carries a duty of thirty-five cents, and a quota is imposed against its export from Canada. Converted into terms of butter this means a duty of eight cents a pound, which I am told means an absolute prohibition. On raw milk, there is no concession whatever; as to poultry, young chickens come into this country on a more favourable basis, from the standpoint of the American producer, than they have had before in recent years. In the result, the farm products that I have mentioned-cereals of all kinds, potatoes, vegetables and vegetable products, butter, eggs, cream, milk, the various dairy products-are not permitted to enter the markets of the United States on any more favourable conditions than they did before, the exception being a limited quantity of green peas, under special circumstances.
Therefore the Canadian farmer is not as well off as he was before, because he is subject to a new competition which he did not previously have to meet. The produce of truck farms-celery, parsnips, carrots, spinach, asparagus-all these commodities now enter our
country under more favourable conditions than before. It is true-and I congratulate the government upon this-that they have accepted what they condemned in days gone by, the policy of the late government in dealing with these matters, namely, in fixing a value which they have not modified except in so far as the agreement compelled them to do so by reducing it by 20 per cent, still maintaining an order in council which gave the authority to the minister, and the minister still exercising that autocratic power which, we were told, threatened the very institutions of our country; he has exercised it. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) smiles; no doubt he is surprised that the country exists at all after the exercise of such autocratic power during the last few weeks by a government avowedly Liberal. There we have the effects upon the farm, vegetables, fruit, matters of that kind. I see a concession here about peas, and a concession there about apples. Apples as a matter of fact constitute an item in which we have to meet the competition of Americans more keenly than that of others.
Now, let us go into the forest. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) has very properly pointed out that there has been a reduction in the tax and in the duty, making together a fifty per cent reduction. One is the tax that expires in June, 1937; the other is the duty of one dollar per thousand. Mr. Hoover, when president of the United States, strongly protested to his committee of, I think it was, ways and means that was then dealing with the tariff of the United States, and as a matter of fact it is well known that the minister to Canada from the United States also protested against the imposition of that tax. But that revenue tax was imposed to the extent of four cents a pound against copper and three dollars a thousand on lumber. Undoubtedly there is an advantage to Canadian lumber dealers in the reduction of that tariff on lumber. I am only sorry that it is not more, and I think it is true that the great consuming public of the United States also regret that it is not more. But let it not be forgotten that this comprises but a very trifling percentage of the whole consumption in the United States; something between five and ten per cent of the entire lumber consumption of that country is covered by the possible exports from Canada. And they are subject to a quota; that must not be forgotten. So far as the products of the forest are concerned we have certain items that enter free now that will be upon the bound list. The one outstanding achievement as far as the agreement is concerned is that

Canada-TJ. S. Trade Agreement
lumber is to have a lower rate than before imposed against it and the tax is to be reduced by fifty per cent.
That exhausts the forest; and from the forest we pass on to the sea. What have we there? Will anyone say that if there were a free vote in this house, regardless of party affiliations or views, this house would regard for a single minute the concessions with respect to fish as being adequate? Would anyone think that Canadians would regard the concessions granted with respect to fish as something that is reasonably, intelligently sound from the standpoint of the Canadian producer? He is denied that market on the Atlantic coast except with respect to some items such as swordfish, and they have to be fresh, not frozen, as I read the item. Now, if there is one objective in the world for which Canadians have struggled, it is to have access to the markets of the United States for their fish. It is the one thing that all governments have sought. In view of what we gave, I suggest that it would not have been unfair for us to have received it. But I am traversing now only what we did not get. So as far as Atlantic fish are concerned we can leave that out. The concessions that we have are those that we already had, except with respect to the item that I have already mentioned, which is, I was going to say, skates, but it is swordfish, which may be consumed in considerable quantities.
We have concessions on the Pacific coast.

Pardon me; I am coming to the Pacific. On the Pacific coast we have concessions with respect to halibut, which I trust will be advantageous to the Canadian fisherman. I observed when I was at Prince Hupert that the Canadian fisherman received Two cents per pound less for his catch than the American, fishing off the same banks, got for his, and the reason was the duty and the fact that the fish were sold in the United States. The local sales are probably insignificant; the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Hanson) can say as to that. The great sales in New England are by the New England Fish Company, shipping their products to Boston, Philadelphia and New York. They used to ship them over the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific. I am told that, with more modern ships, they send the fish to Seattle and the shipment goes from there. The hon. member can verify that.
No; they are still shipped by railroad.
The whole shipment?
The majority. Ninety per cent.

The major shipment still goes by railroad. It used to go by express in a nice refrigerator car attached to the passenger trains. Salmon is a very considerable item, fresh salmon on the east coast and perhaps to a lesser extent fresh salmon on the Pacific coast, for reasons that need not now be discussed. So much for the product of the sea.
Now we come to the products of the mines. Mining has become tremendously important in this country, more and more important, as the Minister of Mines (Mr. Crerar) said the other evening. Show me what we receive from this agreement that is at all commensurate with what we give. It is true that in respect to one or two items covering commodities produced by the aid of electricity, which was one of the points made in the note sent the United States, we receive a reduction of tariff, but in the main there is no change in existing conditions. Of course gold does not pay any duty at any time and last year the major part of our gold found a market in the United States to the extent, I think, of perhaps $95,000,000 altogether. That pays no duty, of course. It has not done so in Canada; it has not done so in the United States.
Then what have we? I did not touch cattle, but we did not get the 50 per cent; we received a concession of only one cent per pound instead of the li cents per pound which would have been the 50 per cent, and even before the president received the powers to which I have referred application was made for the purpose of having the tariff board recommend a reduction of the rate by 50 per cent. That was a case which came to them from Pennsylvania, in which Canadian cattlemen gave their assistance. It will be within the memory of hon. members that we voted the sum of $5,000 to assist in paying the cost of having a Canadian go to Washington, before this government came into office, and as a matter of fact before the late government came into office, in order to make representations in connection with the cattle industry and especially a reduction of tariffs on the principle that the tariff rate was so high that it should be reduced by 50 per cent. That application was dropped when the new provision of the law authorizing the president to enter into agreements came into force. So with respect to the farm, the forest, the sea and the mine we have but two or three items to which to point. They are important, covering lumber and cattle, but what has been the effect with respect to lumber? Only the other

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
day I received a letter saying that the price of lumber has been increased to the Canadian consumer by $2 per thousand while the American consumer is getting his lumber for $2 per thousand less by reason of the agreement.
Not by reason of it.

Yes, by reason of it. The American consumer finds that he is paying S2 per thousand less; therefore he is getting the benefit of that S2. In that case the reduction is passed on to the consumer, but so far as Canada is concerned the reverse is the case. I do not know whether that is general; I have not had before me a sufficiently large number of instances on which to generalize, so I am giving only one or two illustrations.
Is it not a fact that, wages have been increased in the lumber camps of British Columbia; that the cost of the logs is greater and that the $2 has been passed on?

In answer to my hon. friend I may say that I have never known a case in which a producer increased his price when that increase was not caused by higher wages, higher taxes or the like, but they have not always had the same advocacy that has been provided by the hon. gentleman on this occasion.
That is the cause this time.

that the difference in distance between Buffalo and some of out great cities by the actual time consumed in movement by air, to the points of production in Canada is negligible. Therefore, those are two concessions that we have given, involving the loss of revenue on the one hand and the free entry of cut flowers into this country on the other.
The other day an hon. gentleman opposite proved the effect of the concession on magazines when he said that he had been able to obtain a subscription for a famous magazine for fifty cents per year. Of course; they are beginning to offer United States magazines at lower prices than ever before in order to extend their circulation, and the worst of it is that this is not only a concession; it is a concession that cannot be changed. We have pledged our word and honour that during the lifetime of this agreement these magazines will remain free. We have given them the whole intermediate tariff; we have given it for what I have explained and what I have indicated, I trust not unfairly.
We have given our intermediate tariff to our greatest competitor in world trade. Wherever we seek a market, whether it be in Europe or in other parts of the world we have to compete with United States products. Under the intermediate tariff that competition is now met at home. It is here; our Canadian producer has to meet it in his home market. And whatever else may be said, Mr. Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, very properly pointed out that it always seemed to him that the great home market was what had made the United Kingdom as prosperous as it is. Why is the United Kingdom as prosperous as it has been during the last few years? Because it had recourse to a tariff, because British producers provide for the wants of forty million people.
We have built up in this country a structure predicated upon the assumption that the wants of eleven million people shall be provided for by Canadian workmen in Canadian factories, utilizing capital from all over the world. Now that structure is threatened. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), whatever else may be said about his speech the other day, admitted in this house that there had been a lessening of employment, but), he said, only in those cases where there had been high tariffs and new industries had come into operation during the last few years because of the high tariffs imposed by the late government. That is beside the question. The question is: Have we paid too great a price by putting these men out of employment? Where are the commensurate advantages? Where are the advantages that

inure to the Canadian farmer, to the Canadian miner, to the Canadian dairy producer, to the Canadian manufacturer, if eight, ten, fifteen, twenty men go from this factory, from that factory, from yonder factory? As the hon. member for London (Mr. Betts) pointed out this afternoon these are not isolated cases. Industry has been struck in its very vitals by the operation on so wide a scale of the concessions to which I have referred. That might well be something that in more favourable times for the world and for our country in particular we could have faced, but has industry ever faced more critical times than it faces to-day?
The last five years.

I am saying the last
five years and this year. The hon. gentleman either fails to read the ordinary everyday reports that come from time to time or else deliberately does not desire to know, because I am not separating one year from another in talking about this period. In this period has industry ever been so threatened as to-day?
Five years is a period.

Of course it is; it is
a full stop in the ease of the hon. gentleman. Can we afford to have industry so threatened, in a period such as this, when the world has not yet emerged from its depression? There are those who think the world has emerged from the depression, but read the reports; read the reports of the League of Nations; the world is improving; it made great progress in 1935, but the dark days are still with us. I wonder whether the hon. gentleman will take the trouble to read the reports of Canadian industries. They show increasing earnings, it is true, but what do they show in the way of returns on the capital investment? They show very inadequate returns. What is the contrast between England and us?

What do they show
for the working man, the labourer?
Mr. BENNETT': Will you, Mr. Chairman, be good enough to tell that hon. gentleman to talk to himself outside? May I go further and point out that in England every encouragement is given for big profits. The bigger the profits, the better; that is their theoiy. They now make no bones about that. They say that they want industry to make money so that they can get their slice of it to maintain the country. Look at industrial life to-day and consider what our profits tax yields, compared at least with similar taxes in other countries. Banks pay twenty per

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
cent in Great Britain, no one complaining, no one making a hullabaloo, everyone rejoicing, glad that the banks are able to do this, because the state takes so much. In industrial life, if you pick up the reports, you find industrial companies making their final dividends, twelve, fifteen, eighteen per cent, and the state is always glad that is so. But listening to hon. gentlemen during the progress of this discussion one would think nothing was quite so bad as that industry should make money. If hon. gentlemen would only take the trouble to turn up the reports of those industries that they suggest have been so highly protected, and see their returns during the last few years, would they say that those industries have made any money, produced any returns? Their shareholders have been without dividends during this period. Some of them have recently gone on a dividend basis on a small scale, but in the main industry in Canada has not been prosperous. Can we afford at this moment, this period when industry is recovering, to confront it with a form of competition which it has never had to meet before?
The minister the other day said a very fair thing; he said: Look at the intermediate tariff, how high it is; it is not very much different from the general tariff. But that is wholly beside the question. In the United States are industries supplying the wants of 120,000,000 people. To maintain that output ninety per cent of the people are employed to produce for home consumption. The other ten per cent produce a surplus that they can ship to Canada, and so maintain complete capacity as distinguished from limited capacity, and they can afford to sell that ten per cent at low prices and still come within the provisions of our law with respect to dumping without any difficulty, for we gave one other concession I should have mentioned; I wanted to deal with it. We said that we would have no more fixed valuations for duty. Hon. gentlemen cheered loudly when that announcement was made. Well, I wish they had to deal with our problems during the period from 1930 to 1935 when I was in the finance department. There was brought to the office by an industry in Canada a sample felt hat which was offered for sale delivered in Canada at $3.60 a dozen, which was of course less money than we could gather the material for, it being a subsidized product. We put upon it a fixed valuation, a value that bore a proper relation to the cost of production of the article. We say that we provided in our customs act safeguards with respect to duty that would properly care for that. Go to the border cities: what has been
the result there already? Look at the closed doors now that were open in December last.
Hon. gentlemen may say that the automobile industry is not indigenous to this country and we should not have it. But, sir, we have it. The export business to British countries has been enormous under the British preference and the Ottawa agreements. As was mentioned this afternoon, we are selling our goods in every part of the British commonwealth, including New Zealand, Australia, in some instances carrying on much the same business as American industries have been carrying on in Canada with respect to assembling parts. Some countries have provided, as in the case of New Zealand, that there should be some fabrication in their own country by way of completion of the finished article, so that they might supply employment to their own people. That is the position so far as we are concerned.
Those of us who have voted against the agreement certainly have not done so with any joy. I tried to point out something which I know hon. gentlemen opposite do not credit, namely, that I would have infinitely preferred an agreement which I could have supported, and when I make that statement I know I speak for those about me. But we cannot by any process of reasoning convince ourselves that what we are giving is in any way comparable with the benefits we should receive. What we are giving is so much greater than any possible benefits that we cannot give the agreement our support. That is the whole story. If by measuring the agreement in any terms one could use one could arrive at a satisfactory conclusion, I would be satisfied.
I give these illustrations, although very hurriedly, because they are important. The situation resolves itself into this: Can we point to renewed opportunities for work by Canadians in Canada? I have not been here all the time the matter has been under discussion, but I can say that during the time I was here nothing of that kind was done. Certainly my reading of the debates does not show me anything which indicates that by virtue of this agreement any more workmen are to find employment in Canada. But we have the admission that there is a lessening of employment. It is true that the statement is made that there is unemployment in large industries which should not have come into being, because they have had to be supported by too high a tariff.
There is the position. We have a lessening of employment in a period of unexampled unemployment, and with more people on relief than we have had before. That is what we must face. On the other hand we
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

have given to our great competing neighbour not only an opportunity to sell in our market, but an opportunity to sell their surplus products as well, under terms and conditions which we did not think possible before. A year or two ago I gave illustrations to show that prices fixed for duty purposes did no more than give Canadians the measure of protection they had under the tariff, before exchange values had so altered. I took the pound at S3.76; I took it at $4.00, and I was able to show that unless we had done what we did, in view of the terms in our tariff, we would be giving our goods practically no protection at all. With respect to the United States, where the general tariff prevailed, the same condition was equally true. Now, having abolished any provision for fixing values for duty purposes we still say that we have adequately protected the situation. I think it will be found that that is not by any means so. We have abolished any opportunity to do that which was our very safeguard, and all that stood between us and irretrievable ruin in Canada at one time, because the relation between goods and our exchange was so intimate and so closely allied that we had to take the steps we did to preserve our position. I might say something about exchange, but I shall not do so to-day.
I wish to say only one thing more, and that is that we have increased competition and have lessened the opportunity for the Canadian workman. We have been given no corresponding benefits, except in the manner I have mentioned, and they were in the very nature of things such as we might expect, in any event, under the application of the flexible provisions of the American tariff existing prior to the power given to the president in 1934.
We have done more. We have lessened the possibility of the establishment of new industries in Canada. Listening to addresses made with respect to mineral development, how can one do more than hope for a great improvement in the industrial life of this country? But we have lessened the opportunity. Why? Because we have said to Japan that when production in Canada is not equal to ten per cent of the consumption it is not an article made or produced in this dominion. That applies to every country having favoured nation treatment; it applies to the United States. Now, the industry in Canada which is not producing ten per cent of Canadian consumption is no longer producing an article made in Canada, and cannot launch out in support of itself. Therefore it has no choice; such industries will never be established.
They will still have the tariff.

No. I am pointing out we are seriously restricted in applying protection in the case of Japan, with respect to goods not made in Canada. Goods not made in Canada are now defined as goods the production of which is not equal to ten per cent of our consumption. That is going to apply to every country of the world enjoying favoured nation treatment. We have defined that which during all these years we declined to define. In the days of Tupper, Macdonald, Laurier, Borden and Meighen, and in later days, the Canadian government declined to define the term "of a class or kind made in Canada." It is true that there were rules in the customs administration, and that it was stated that the rules were applied to meet given situations, because we were endeavouring to develop industry in Canada. Now, for the first time we have given a definition. We have declared that unless ten per cent of a given product consumed in Canada is made in this country, then it is not a product produced in Canada. Japan, with her low rate of exchange, is to have the market to herself. Or the market may go to other countries; it will be divided among them, because unless production in Canada is equal to ten per cent of consumption the article is not produced in Canada. We have defined what in days gone by we never undertook to define,-what, I must say, the late government declined to define.
Then, there is one last argument: Look at what we have done for the instruments of production. I wonder whether there is any member of the committee who has not read with some degree of apprehension what took place in Russia in the last seven or eight years, or what takes place in all countries developing industrial life. The very first thing they do is to provide means whereby within their own countries they can manufacture instru-mets of production. Why were tractors one of the first articles made in Russia? Because they must have tractors made in their own country so that they will not be dependent upon foreigners for their supply. I could give case after case to the committee indicating where we Canadians have found ourselves desperately handicapped because we have had to go to foreign countries to get instruments of production. I could do more than that. I can say that in the development of the oil fields in the Turner valley interests which occupied a strategic or preferred position were able to get their instruments of production

Caiuxda-U. S. Trade Agreement
from Pittsburgh more readily than, were others who were endeavouring in their own way to carry on operations.
Take some of the very oldest firms in Canada who have been endeavouring to produce instruments of production, in the mining field, for instance, Bertrams, if you will, or Ingersoll-Rand, a branch in the eastern townships of that great concern in the United States, as well as many others I could name. What has been the whole purpose? The purpose has been that Canadians might be self-sufficient, and I use that word gladly. The purpose was that Canadians should within their own borders produce the instruments to enable them to develop the vast resources of this country. But place yourself in a position where you are no longer able to produce those instruments; then you are at the caprice of your competing neighbour, and you will obtain your instruments of production when he is good and ready to give them to you. And, remember, his own people get them first.
Why did w7e ever establish an agricultural implement business in Canada? Everyone knows why. There will be no doubt in the minds of hon. members on that point if they will read the debates of that time. Our endeavour has been, not only in that respect, but wherever we have undertaken to develop our resources, either minerals or mines or whatever it may be, farm lands or anything else, to try to provide for the production of instruments in our own country. The other day the hon. member for Huron North referred to the fact that someone had bought an instrument of production in Burlington cheaper than he otherwise would because he paid less duty. And so he did. How much less will he get for his fruit next fall? That is the question. How much less will he get by reason of the very competition provided for by this agreement? And what about the other man whose cattle found1 their way to the market in Buffalo? Ever since the AAA was held unconstitutional in the United States the price of cattle has fallen until, the week before last, you could not ship cattle to the United States as against Canadian prices and make a profit.
What we have endeavoured to do by slow degrees has been to make this country selfsufficient, and it has been an uphill struggle, living as we do in this northern climate, with a limited population. We have endeavoured, with these great resources which we hold in trust, to develop them according to a plan which would ensure some compensation being given the western farmer for what he said was the increased price he may have paid for his implements of production. We have ensured him his home market by every means in our power, and I have pointed out what that means. I have pointed out how vastly important that market is. While the United States export trade amounts to ten or twelve per cent it has nevertheless exercised a profound influence upon the national life of that country. In Canada our export trade, apart from consumption at home, amounts to fifteen, seventeen and sometimes twenty per cent, and that is of enormous importance to the national life of this dominion.
We must develop here not the doctrine of isolation but the doctrine of self-sufficiency as against those countries that compete with us, not on the principle of doing unto others as you would that they should do unto you; not on the principle enunciated by Sam Slick the clockmaker, but on the principle of David Harum, "Do it first." Do unto others as they are about to do unto you, but do it first. For surely you cannot argue that this young country, with a population of eleven millions, should lower its tariff and so open a field for the activities of others, itself desisting from the development of its own industry in the manufacture of instruments of production, and depending on someone else. No; by every means within our power we have endeavoured to bring about a balanced economy so that all might receive the benefits of that system and that tariffs-whatever differences of opinion we might have respecting them-should be of advantage to every interest in the country. In this instance, however, we have departed from that principle and have granted concessions that are out of all proportion to the benefits which we are to receive. For those benefits that we have received I rejoice with others. But I cannot contemplate paying too high a price for them, half a million dollars here, half a million or a million there. I cannot contemplate such a situation with equanimity unless I see somewhere else some means by which we shall receive half a million or a million and a half in return.
My right hon. friend will no doubt say that I look upon this matter from the standpoint of bargaining, in too haggling a spirit, forgetting the large view that may be taken of good neighbourliness. Well, I read the other day what has happened with respect to good neighbours on this continent for the last hundred years, and we have never been lacking in the expression of willingness to be good neighbours. We have however been unwilling to be good neighbours for the purpose of having our country exploited in the name of good neighbourliness. That has been our position, and it is the position we still take. I am not at all concerned about the
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

Mr. Chairman, I have just listened to the case put up by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) against the benefits accruing to this country from this trade agreement. In that conjectural brief, so to speak, which he put forward, it will be noticed that the right hon. gentleman gave no concrete example. The consumer was not mentioned from beginning to end of his remarks although the secondary industries were.
I should like to give a concrete example of the benefits of the Japanese treaty to a basic industry. Only to-day I was talking to a well-informed lumberman from the maritime provinces and he told me that the effects of the Japanese treaty have been felt already by the lumber dealers. It is an indirect effect, but it does exist. At one time Japan took a considerable quantity of the lumber produced by British Columbia. When the Japanese market was shut off, this British Columbia lumber came into competition in England with lumber from the maritime provinces. As a result of the treaty with Japan, British Columbia is now able to get her lumber into that market and the result has been that the whole cut for next year in the maritimes has already been contracted for in England. My authority for making this statement is quite good and I stand to be corrected by hon members from British Columbia. This is a concrete example. It is not a case of saying, "I am apprehensive," or "I am afraid." It is a concrete example of what the Japanese treaty has done for Canada; it is not leaving to conjecture what may happen or what will happen.

The Minister of Trade
and Commerce (Mr. Euler) is not in his place, but he directed my attention to the fact that an observation I made during the afternoon might be misunderstood. He thought that possibly the committee gathered that I said if goods were not of a class or kind made in Canada they would enter free. If I did I should have finished the sentence and said, free of dumping duty. I desire to make that perfectly clear. The tariff is not changed by reason of the provision in the Japanese arrangement whereby commodities not manufactured in Canada to the extent of ten per cent of Canadian consump-. tion are regarded as goods not made in Canada. If Canadian production is ten per
cent or less than Canadian consumption, then such goods, I repeat, are regarded as goods not made in Canada, but if production is more than ten per cent of Canadian consumption then they are to be regarded as goods of a class or kind made in Canada. In one instance they would pay dumping duty and in the other instance they would be free from dumping duty, but in both cases subject to the tariff as provided by statute. I desire to make that abundantly clear. I told the minister that I would do so as soon as the committee resumed this evening.

Well, Mr. Chairman, this afternoon we listened to a very able address setting forth the Conservative view of the agreement, and I think it may be said that an address of that type by a very able advocate constitutes the full case against the agreement. At this stage I do not desire to impede the progress of the measure through the house by again going over in detail matters which were thoroughly discussed when the house was in committee of ways and means on the schedule. Of course it was to be expected, the right hon. leader of the opposition being unavoidably absent during a portion of that period, that he would summarize the objections of his party in an address such as we heard this afternoon, and when a great advocate starts to view with alarm then the viewing with alarm is thoroughly done and we all get a feeling that something terrible is going to happen, that as
a result of what we are about to do Canadian employment will be seriously reduced. For a time we are tempted to forget the facts in listening to the "view with alarm" eloquence of such an advocate.
But certain facts have been disclosed even in the relatively short period during which this agreement has been in effect. I admit that an experience of a month or two is not a criterion, but I submit that it is very much more of a criterion than the calamitous prophecies of the right hon. leader of the opposition. For instance, in the matter of employment I cannot, nor can any other member of this committee, follow the fluctuations in employment and the reasons therefor in every large or small industrial plant from one end of the dominion to the other. There may be cases, indeed I know there are some, in which the trade agreement is being used as an excuse for letting out men, whereas, as a matter of fact, competitive and other conditions within Canada are the real reasons, in some cases at least that have come to the attention of the government.
In connection with industry as a whole, however, some information is available. No one, I think, would accuse the Vancouver Province of being unduly friendly towards the present government or likely to misrepresent facts in a manner which would favour a measure proposed by this government. But in the Vancouver Province of January 11 I find this headline:
Better Days in B.C. Mills

Screaming saws, rising employment figures and a steady stream of lumber trucks from the majority of Vancouver sawmills are giving rise to hopes that the lumbering business will soon step into higher gear. If a bill is called an Income War Tax bill, or anything of the kind, it should meet war expenditures, soldiers' pensions, expenditures of the Department of National Defence, and like expenditures. My point is that when measures are provided to meet expenditures resulting from war they should not be made to apply to civil expenditures. Therefore I suggest that there should be a change in the accounting of the Department of Finance. I do not know whether you were in the house, sir, but I made the suggestion to the last Minister of Finance who replied that the matter would be referred to his successor in office. I take this opportunity to submit the same observations to the present minister, in order that he may take advantage of the suggestion.
All government revenues go into a melting pot. War taxes of every description should meet war expenditures of every description; otherwise it is obtaining money under false pretences. For many years by governments which held office before the war expenditures were made for public works, railways and canals, agriculture, and so on. Since the war there have been special expenditures. Therefore, as some of this legislation has been drafted because of the war, I suggest that the accounting in the Department of Finance should take that fact into consideration. In my humble view I am perfectly in order when I make this suggestion to the minister.
There have been made in the Department of National Defence expenditures which cannot be justified before the people of Canada, and for that reason I do not see how moneys can be derived from an Income War Tax Act. If the expenditure is one resulting from the war I do not object to it, but I suggest that those who have been in the service of His Majesty should not receive preferential treatment. Let us look at the bill. It is entitled Income War Tax Act (special tax), and imposes a special tax on certain people.

Now, I do not see how that tax can be put into the melting pot of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada, out of which to provide a higher superannuation for some former officials of the Department of National Defence who have taken advantage of being seconded from that department to another one in order to receive a higher superannuation than the ordinary civil servant of this country receives, and as the money that is to be provided by the legislation now before us is to be used in part for such a purpose, I must tell the committee what is going on. I must do so, because several members of this committee have been asking me repeatedly, " What is the matter with McNaughton? What is the matter with Steel "? They were told: We will appoint you to the bench at such and such a salary. Upon that understanding the judges were ready to sacrifice the clientele that they had built up in a life's practice, in order to sit on the bench to serve their fellow-countrymen to the best of their ability.
