subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES

speechtext:
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting relief for unemployment and assistance for agricultural settlement and rehabilitation and development of natural and other resources, and to provide for such payments out of the consolidated revenue fund as may be necessary for all or any of the purposes of the proposed legislation.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Bothwell in the chair.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
This resolution precedes
the introduction of a bill which will supersede the Relief Act of 1935. Beginning with the autumn session of 1930 parliament has been asked annually to approve legislation to authorize the government of the day to employ funds of the dominion for the relief of such of our population as may be in necessitous circumstances through prevailing unemployment and crop conditions. The

present resolution precedes the introduction of the Unemployment and Relief Assistance Act, 1936, which is designed to provide similar authority for the forthcoming fiscal year.
The relief of distress has always been held by the dominion to be primarily a responsibility of the provincial and municipal authorities, with the proviso that where the need for relief has been such as to place a very severe burden upon the provinces and municipalities it is proper and necessary that the dominion government should extend financial aid to the other governmental authorities. This principle we propose should be continued under the present measure. Accordingly it provides the requisite authority for agreement between the dominion and the provinces with respect to relief measures, unemployment relief works, and loans, advances and guarantees to the provinces. With respect to dominion-provincial agreements the bill provides the same general subject matter as heretofore. It is also proposed that the governor in council may enter into agreements with corporations, partnerships and individuals engaged in industry, respecting the expansion of industrial employment. In addition to the provision for works and undertakings in agreement with others, authority is proposed to give the governor in council power to authorize dominion works and undertakings out of moneys appropriated by parliament.
In pursuance of a policy of parliamentary control of expenditures the proposed bill provides that agreements entered into with the provinces respecting relief measures are to be approved by resolution of the House of Commons as well as by the governor in council, and similar provision has been inserted covering agreements with corporations, partnerships and individuals engaged in industry. As a further safeguard to parliamentary control the bill has reference throughout, in so far as new commitments are involved, only to moneys appropriated by parliament, which will be asked to vote funds necessary for these purposes. It may be recalled that the Relief Act of 1935 gave the governor in council wide powers, under the general heading of peace, order and good government, and also as regards protection of the financial position of the dominion and provinces.
Similar provisions are not contained in the new measure. Such general provisions affecting the making of regulations by the governor in council, the appointment of staff, the publication of orders in council, and the report to parliament, are comparable with similar provisions in the act of 1935. The bill would expire on March 31, 1937, except

Unemployment
where in the nature of things obligations under this or earlier relief acts must be carried forward. I do not intend at this time to engage in a more extended exposition of the bill. That will be reserved for a later stage. My observations at this time are intended only to be explanatory, and I hope I have met the reasonable expectations of the house in that regard.

speechtext: I can hardly think my ears correctly reported what I heard. It cannot be possible that a Liberal minister could have suggested what I have heard to-night. After what we heard in this country during the months of September and October, is it possible that a government contemplates giving aid to industry and entering into contracts with individuals and corporations to enable them to expand their business? Surely my hearing must have deceived me. It cannot be possible that the government has done this! No wonder the Minister of Finance laughs; he has to find the money to foot the bill. He had no idea, nor had anybody else, that a Liberal minister would ever do this. Why-

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Better let me speak for myself.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
The interference with
business that wras taking place in former days is mild, compared with what the hon. gentleman has just said. "We are not going to do it with tariffs; we are going to do it with bonuses." "We are not going to do it with bonuses, we are going to make agreements with individuals, with companies and with corporations to enable them to expand their business, and to carry on, regardless of what the consequences may be to the people's finances." Surely there is something wrong. The hon. gentleman should have been a minister in the former administration, for the doctrine he has now promulgated was the doctrine that was condemned on every platform in Canada during the last election campaign.
But that is not all. The unfortunate part about it is that this resolution does not authorize anything such as the hon. gentleman has stated. There could be nothing clearer than that the resolution should at least lay the foundation for the bill. On one occasion I found myself in exactly the same position, because I had not sufficiently amplified in the resolution what I proposed the measure should be. Show me in the resolution any provision which contemplates (a) a loan to a province or (b) a guarantee of a loan to a province. That will be found in the Relief
Act of 1935. The hon. gentleman says that he contemplates doing that, but he cannot do it in a bill founded on this resolution. He has to have another resolution to do that. There is nothing clearer, as was pointed out to me when I was learning the tools of the profession, that the resolution must make clear every object contemplated in the bill. It may do it in general terms.
Let us look at the resolution. It states:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting relief for unemployment-
That is fair and simple. Then it goes on: -and assistance for agricultural settlement and rehabilitation and' development of natural and other resources.
That is clear. "Agricultural settlement and rehabilitation"-I am going to ask the minister, before we leave the committee stage, to give us an explanation of what he means by that expression. Then, in the third place we have the "development of natural and other resources." We have not heard anything about that. Perhaps the Minister of Mines (Mr. Crerar) in his expansiveness, proposed to open up some gold mines and use this relief money for that purpose. Paradventure he is going to engage in the development of the coke industry, or possibly the peat industry, or possibly some other industry of that type. But we should have an explanation with regard to that.
As the resolution reads it contemplates the development of natural and other resources. Now, by "other resources" of course the minister must mean the building of breakwaters, bridges and works of that kind. But let us go a step further:
-and to provide for such payments out of the cosolidated revenue fund-
Without limitation, without saying how much. It is absolutely essential, if we are going to found a bill upon a resolution, to give the limitation; otherwise it is a blank cheque. Then:
-as may be necessary for all or any of the purposes of the proposed legislation.
In other words, here is your blank cheque, again.

I did not quite follow the hon. member when he spoke about the governor in council approving, approving, approving and approving. As far as I could see it was a governor in council measure, for never have I heard an explanation of a resolution where there were more references to the governor in council, the governor in council, the governor in council, not in the resolution itself, but in the explanation with respect to it. Therefore I would judge that the governor in council which was so much out of favour a few months ago, or years ago, is now very much in favour.
Then there is added the provision that the house will approve these matters, ex post facto, or antecedently. It can only approve them when the house is in session, or after they have been approved. If they are approved by the governor in council and also by the House of Commons, this would mean of course that the house could approve only such plans as had been made before the house rose. After that, the house could approve them after they had been carried into effect, and I suppose a majority could always be relied upon, as a matter of form.
But I assure the minister that when he speaks of the approval of the governor in council and then the approval of the House of Commons there should be something more than the anticipation of a rubber-stamp approval. That used to be one of the grounds of contention. Now, are we to have approval of these things by the House of Commons before they are entered into, or after they are performed? It would be a lot of value if it was done after, would it not? It would be like locking the stable door after the horse had been stolen.
Then, there is a further point. I am pointing out that that is all that is covered by the resolution. The hon. gentleman stated that it was intended that the House of Commons should approve arrangements that might be made with industries. Well, if that is so it becomes tremendously important that there should be mention of it in the resolution. There should be mention that the expenditure should be subject to the direction of the House of Commons, either before or after it is made.
Inasmuch as the Prime Minister stated on Friday that the next item of business to be taken up would be the second reading of a bill respecting harbours, I suggest that the minister move that the committee rise for tonight. He is dealing with an item of travelling expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I heard the hon. member for Portage la Prairie make the statement in the house, but I never had any idea that he was attempting to show that the members of the late government had spent $18,000,000 on travelling expenses. What I gathered was that he was speaking of the travelling expenses of the whole dominion government service for those five years.
That is not the government service; that is the service of the Dominion of Canada.
I never expected the house to believe that I meant the ministers of the government had spent that amount of money.
What does it mean?

I said, and I repeat my statement: Over $19,500,000 was spent by the late government between 1930 and 1935, and that includes all departments, including the Department of Agriculture, mentioned by the leader of the opposition. All the right hon. gentleman has to do is to look up the auditor general's report and he will find that my figures are correct.

Not only am I now
satisfied that an attempt was made to leave an impression that was not warranted, but it was stated directly in the dispatch which was sent to the newspapers. Particulars were given for the year ended March 31, 1930, the government having come into office on August 7, 1930. The total for that year was over $4,000,000. There was a diminution the next year; there was a diminution the next year

Supply-Marine-Pilotage
and a diminution the next year. This item would be included in that sum and it would include the mounted police and all other services. It was not expended by the government. It represented the vote of this house; it represented estimates passed for that purpose. The government submitted estimates to the house and the house passed them. The figures were so transparently erroneous and the cheers with which the observations of the hon. member were greeted showed what it was done for. Sooner or later we shall have the right to ask-

I rise to a point of order. Surely the leader of the opposition has not the right to impute to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie an attempt to mislead the house. The right hon. gentleman said, " An attempt to leave an impression that was not warranted by the facts." I submit that the right hon. gentleman has no right .to say that the hon. member for Portage la Prairie attempted to mislead this house, and I ask for a ruling that he is out of order.

The hon. member apparently missed the point. I was referring to the newspaper report sent out and I can give him the headlines that appeared about this statement of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. The rules of the house provide that I can place a question on the order paper, if I so desire, asking for particulars. I certainly propose to continue to ask the hon. gentleman what he did mean by that statement. Anyone reading the statement made that evening, without its being amplified as it was by the Minister of Finance, would draw only one conclusion; anyone reading the newspaper would draw only one conclusion, that the government had expended for travelling expenses this particular sum of money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is so absurd.

A gentleman wrote me
to say that he was quite perturbed at seeing the statement that this amount of money had been spent in travelling expenses during the past five years by the ministers, $4,000,000 being expended in one year.

I rise to a point of order.
I submit that the right hon. gentleman has no right to say that certain statements were calculated to leave a wrong impression. The right hon. gentleman has said that the hon. member for Portage la Prairie made a statement calculated to mislead this house and I submit that he has no right to make such an implication against the hon. member. I ask for a ruling on that.

If I may be allowed to
reply-
If the hon. member is speaking to a point of order he is in order.

Speaking to a point of
order, I am not an experienced parliamentarian; I am only an ordinary farmer from western Canada. I have no objection to what the right hon. leader of the opposition has stated here to-night. I do not care what motives he imputes; he is wrong. What I meant to convey to the people of Canada was that we might save something in the cost of administration, and when I gave those figures out of the auditor general's report- and they are true, notwithstanding the remarks of the right hon. gentleman-I wanted the people of this country to note what it is costing in travelling expenses and everything else. I think that is what he is objecting to. If it will soothe his feelings, I should like him to go to the auditor general's report for the five years previous-
I have.

-and he will find that the travelling expenses are larger. But the trouble is that the people of Canada who pay the shot do not know these things, and what I am trying to do is to let them know, not to say anything derogatory of the late government or anyone else; that is not in my nature. But I reserve the right, as a member of this house
Order.
-to convey some information to the Canadian people when I think it is necessary to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On the point of order, it seems to me to rest entirely on the question of what the leader of the opposition did say. If he said that a certain newspaper article was calculated to leave a certain impression, that is one thing. If he stated, as the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) has stated, that a member of this house made a statement with a certain object, thus imputing a motive to that member, then the leader of the opposition was clearly out of order.
No; he was not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I doubt very much if we shall know precisely what the facts are until we read Hansard in the morning. In the meantime I suggest, for the purpose of
Supply-Marine-Pilotage

getting on with the business, that the point of order be withdrawn; the leader of the opposition be satisfied with the discussion so far, and we proceed with the discussion of the estimates.

I accept the suggestion
of the Minister of Finance.

I was dealing with the question at this time because it is the first opportunity I had, when the item regarding travelling expenses came before the committee. This item, the minister says, includes an item for travelling expenses in connection with lighthouse and pilot service, and he says that under this head, namely administration of pilotage, there has been a reduction of $28,000 partly caused by a lessening of travelling expenses. Perhaps the hon. minister would be good enough to indicate just what is meant by travelling expenses, for I should like to assure the committee that there is set out in the auditor general's report the details of the expenditure of each department, on the one hand being the appropriation and on the other the expenditures, and if any member can suggest a method by which there can be a saving in any of these expenditures I am quite sure the Minister of Finance will be the most pleased man in the world. I assure the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) as well as other hon. members that the estimates voted by parliament for this purpose during the last five years were very much less than they were during the preceding five years, and that the reduction was to a point at which it was contended at times there was hardly sufficient to carry on the public service. If there is any suggestion that money can be saved I am sure the minister will be glad and the Minister of Finance as well. For instance, in connection with the conveyance of prisoners to the penitentiaries, in connection with the movement of the mounted! police, in connection with the transfer of trade officers from one section to another, in connection with movements of officials who have duties to perform, in connection with inspections of various kinds, if savings can be effected I am sure the ministers will be gratified. But as regards this item I should like to know just what was saved in travelling expenses, because this is the first opportunity we have had to discuss it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The item is for miscellaneous printing and travelling; it is rather difficult to sort it out. The item that is being voted this year in the amount of $90,600

is roughly the net expenditure that has been made in the last three or four years. That expenditure in 1032-33 was $86,812, in 1033-34 about the same, in 1034-35 about the same; in 1935-36 up to January 31, $92,765. It has been the practice in a good many places to loan money to pilots pending receipt of pilotage dues. That practice has been gradually cut down, due to the fact that we found it possible to collect the dues more promptly, and the vote this year provides no such sum for that purpose. I think that is the explanation of the reduction.

The question I was
asking the minister was: What reduction has there been in travelling expenses under this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
We are allowing for these
various items to include travelling expenses for all districts, examination of pilots, printing and stationery, electric current, telephone, laundry, repairs and freight charges, fuel for Father Point station, repairs to buildings, et cetera. This year we are allowing $3,883, while last year the allowance was $16,800, I think that undoubtedly the difference enters in the item of repairs to buildings, et cetera; I imagine some extensive repairs were made.
It is a bulk item, as the minister says, but is there any specific saving with respect to travelling expenses, and what was spent for travelling expenses last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We do not have that. They are very minor. Just places where the pilot is dropped some distance and he has to get back.

Do I understand that
this covers merely the administration charges of the pilot service to all harbours of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is all.

There can be very little
travelling expenses coming under administration, surely.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Very little; there are some
expenses.

Travelling of the pilots
does not come in.

I note that the leader of the opposition made reference to a saving of $28,000 as compared with last year. If I understood the Minister of Marine correctly, he stated that that was about the same amount as had been spent during the past three or four years. I would point out that

Supply-M arine-Pilotage
the estimates of 1933, on page 42, show the amount as 1218,000. This year the amount is $96,000, which would mean a difference of $122,000, So I think we should congratulate ourselves that we have a minister who can in such a short time bring about such a saving. I do not say that the amount was expended, but it certainly shows in the estimate, as quoted by me, as $218,000. May I inquire as to the fees or salaries paid1 under this particular item, whether there is a salary system in all the ports or whether there is a fee and salary combination system being used, and whether any consideration has been given to a change from the fee system to a straight salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This particular vote provides for certain salaries that are paid by the department. In addition there are fees that are paid to the pilots and that cover the pilotage dues. I can give those if the hon. member is interested.

No; I am not particularly
concerned about the amounts. I am concerned about the system under which the minister operates, whether he considers the out-and-out salary better than the way he is now conducting the pilotage service, under a fee and salary system.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The administration only is covered by salaries. We provide, for instance, a head office at Ottawa with a superintendent of pilots; similarly we have offices in Vancouver, Halifax, Saint John, Quebec, Montreal and Kingston. We have an office there in each of those cities; we rent or own an office, and we have a certain staff such as stenographers and others. This covers that particular service. In addition to that there is a system of pilotage fees paid by the boats, and those fees are distributed among the pilots.
In that connection I should like to ask who determines the amount of the fee to be charged by the pilot.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: An order in council of the government, fixed by law.

Then, may I ask, just apart
from this item, though I believe it has a close connection, whether undter the new bill the national harbour board will have authority to regulate the charges or fees to be paid to the pilots in the various ports?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No; the fees for pilots are fixed by the Canada Shipping Act. which is administered by the Department of Marine. That has nothing to do with harbour board legislation.

I should like to bring one other
point to the attention of the minister. The contention has been advanced on more than one occasion that the fee charged in some cases is altogether too high. I have particularly in mind the fee for pleasure craft belonging to United States tourists who visit various ports. They claim that they are charged a rather high fee, and that it prevents quite a number from entering our ports and spending money that otherwise would be spent in this country. I should like to hear what the minister has to say in regard to this point.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I am told by my officers that it has been brought to the attention of the department, though it has not been brought to my attention. As to pilotage fees in general, however, I must say that they seem to be reasonable; the pilots make only an earning which I would consider as reasonable for the class of work they do. In regard to pleasure boats, I shall be very glad to look into that question and see if any differential can be set up.

I should not like to leave the impression that I am objecting to the fees earned by the pilots in any port. They have a hard time and a hard life, but I was wondering whether in some way another system might be arranged under which they would receive a proper remuneration but not on the fee basis. That was the thought I had in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I may say that pilotage all over the world is on a fee basis, and I think our rates are quite in order. Every cent that is collected in fees goes to the pilots themselves. There is no charge for overhead at all; we carry that. These fees are pooled and distributed to the pilots.

Some hon. members who have spoken have quoted rather large figures, much larger than those of this year or last year, as appearing in the estimates in different years. I gathered from what the minister said that over a period of five years the expenditures had been practically the same. Could the minister give us the expenditures for the last four or five years?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext: Does the government build pilot boats or loan money to pilots to build their boats, or is anything of that kind done?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes; we have loaned money to pilots in Halifax, Sydney and Saint John to build their boats, and they have paid it back on a fee basis.
Does that come out of this grant?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It has come out of this grant. There is none outstanding at the moment; it has been paid back.
Item agreed to.

Salaries, including amounts required to pay allowances to office appliance operators, grade 2, operating mechanical audit card punching machines in accordance with the terms of order in council P.C. 280/383, dated February 17,	1930; to pay allowances to
typists, grade 1, employed cutting stencils in accordance with regulations approved by order in council; and to pay allowances to office appliance operators, grade 2, in the revenue division employed' as key punch operators, schedules and rates to be decided upon by the Civil Service Commission and the Post Office department and approved by the governor in council, $1,248,660.
Contingencies, $155,920.

There will be a great deal of discussion on this item, with regard to the dismissal of officials and matters of that ltind. It will be a long, controversial item, because it covers everything in connection with the Post Office Department. Perhaps the minister will say what is included under the item ; that would be a good start, and then we can go on.

In this item is included all that is found at page 92 of the estimates; it is the civil government item. If members of the committee will just glance down the two columns they will find that in most cases they are the same. There are certain items in which there is a difference, but as a general rule they are practically the same except that there is an increase, as my hon. friends will see, amounting to $30,562 in civil government salaries.
Those are statutory increases?

Those are
statutory increases, and I assume that my right hon. friend will be fairly familiar with the circumstances leading up to them. If it

is the wish of the committee I can give the details which make up that net increase. There are 358 statutory increases amounting to $24,060. To provide for the reestablishment of six positions abolished by order in council-
What six positions are they ?

One departmental accountant, grade 3, at a salary of $3,060; one principal clerk, $1,920; three clerks, grade 3, at $1,380, making a total of $4,140; one clerk, grade 2, at $1,200. That makes a total of $10,320. I may say that these positions were abolished under orders in council authorizing staff control regulations, and the restoration of the positions was approved by the civil service commission and authorized by order in council dated September 16, 1935. Then there is one additional position of stenographer, grade 2, at $1,260. That is to provide for Miss G. Fournier, who is employed as clerk, grade 4, in the office of the former Postmaster General. The creation of this position was also authorized by .order in council.
And by the civil service commission?

Yes. Then
there is an allowance for private secretary, $600; that is the usual allowance. Those make a total of $36,240. From that take $5,678 for decreases. The difference between salaries of employees who left the service and the amount required for those who replace them was $2,400; then the current salary reduction is $3,278, making $5,678 off the $36,240, which leaves $30,562. That deals with the first part of that item.

That is entirely satisfactory as far as I am concerned. I thought that included also some employees in the outside service. There is only an increase of seven as far as that is concerned, and these seven have been explained; they were temporaries before under the order in council and they have been restored to their permanent position by approval of the civil service commission and by order in council. I think that is the position.
That is correct.
It is not this item.

No; I will not insist now,
but when we come to item 263 perhaps I shall request the Postmaster General to go into it a little more fully.

I shall be
glad to.

That is the item under
which the discussion to which the hon. member refers took place last year.

Under the item of contingencies we have clerical and other assistance. What is the nature of that, in addition to that provided for in the larger vote of $1,248,660? The vote I have mentioned seems to provide for all sorts of clerks and messengers and clerical assistants. What is this?

My hon. friend will notice that under contingencies there is a decrease of $16,800. That is made up of a decrease of $15,000 on printing and stationery and $1,800 on sundries. Last year it was $172,720 and this year it is estimated at $155,920.

What I was asking was an explanation of the first heading, clerical and other assistance $75,920, the same as last year. I would like to know where that expenditure comes in, what that includes in addition to the item of civil government.
That includes all the temporary employees, including the Christmas rush and everything of that nature.
In Ottawa, or all through the country?
Ottawa only.
Shall the item carry?
No; the contingencies item we have not dealt with.
That is what we are dealing with now.
Printing and stationery, there is a reduction there.
In printing and stationery there is a reduction of $15,000.

A moment ago the
minister said something about temporary employees for the Ottawa Christmas rush. Will he tell us how those employees are selected?

The civil
service commission has an eligible list, and it is from that list first of all that the Christmas rush employees are selected, if my memory serves me aright.
No; I think that is not quite right.
I mean for delivering mail on city routes. Is the minister referring to that?

No; there is a difference between those engaged for the Christmas rush and those engaged at headquarters for other services. The ordinary Christmas rush employees relate generally to the handling and delivery of mail. Then there are others for making out money orders, and other duties requiring a certain amount of help. The great part, however, is the delivery of extra mail at Christmas time.
Supply-Post Office
To what branch of the extra service is the minister referring?
The financial branch at headquarters.
The minister does not refer to the temporary employees who deliver mail on the routes?
No.
Who is responsible for the appointment of temporary help at Christmas time?
The civil service commission.
Is that right?
That was not my impression.
Is the hon. member speaking about the headquarters staff, or is he speaking generally?
Generally.

That does not come under this item, although I would have no objection to discussing it. We are now dealing with the inside service. Those engaged for the Christmas rush are selected from the eligible list for the inside service. In the outside service they are selected partly from the eligible list and partly from the-
Patronage list.

Selections
made under the direction of the postmaster.
No one but the Postmaster General has anything to do with the selection of the extra help?
I assume he gets all the information he can from the various parties upon whom he feels he can rely.
He always gets it from reliable sources.
He gets the best staff he can. There seems to be an impression that help for the Christmas rush is a position which should be given to a person not able to do anything else.
Except vote.

That is not
the case.
Providing he belongs to the political party in power, Mr. Minister.
They are paid pretty good wages for the hours they work. They are required to work long hours and to work diligently. It is necessary that they be able-bodied young men.

I did not ask the question out of idle curiosity. Last Christmas season a number of men who had been employed alleged that they were not reemployed, but that an entirely new group of men had been taken on. It looked to me as though there might have been some political patronage lurking in the background.
Can the minister tell the committee the number of extra help employed this Christmas as compared with the year before?

I think some hon. members are confusing this item with another one. This one, I believe, refers only to head office and has not anything to do with employment outside of Ottawa. It has to do with a number of employees brought in to give a hand because of a rush of business, and because of the terrific strain upon head office officials during the Christmas season. It is to provide suitable employment for those who, if they did not receive it, would be greatly aggrieved. The eligible list, so-called, is a list held by the civil service commission of those who are willing to take a job in the public service, if they get a chance. It is from that list that these people are drawn. There is no doubt that this does not apply to other than Ottawa. The item for contingencies touches only Ottawa?
That is correct.
Nobody else?
No.

I am told that
is for travelling expenses of head office officials.
Quite so.
During the whole year.
Are they travelling all the time, or do they work at head office?

They are just travelling while they are on the road.

Supply-Post Office

It is only fair to say that the regulations under which these men travel have been approved by successive governments. It provides that if they have free transportation they shall not receive payment. Some of the higher officials have free transportation. They receive so much a day, or they have to produce vouchers. In every sense the expenditures are regulated and in the end they are audited by the auditor general before they can possibly be paid out.
Yes.
That is it, in order that there may be no misunderstanding.
One of my colleagues has referred me to pages 92 and 93 of the estimates. Is that correct?
Yes.
This is a most interesting department. I have received numerous letters from my constituents respecting changes of post offices and changes in regard to mail contracts.	,

I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member, but I must tell
him that mail contracts do not come under this item.

There is a connection
between the inside and outside services. Every order the outside service receives comes from the inside service at Ottawa. Those two items should be studied together. For instance, a postmaster may give unsatisfactory service. In that event I would write the secretary, the deputy minister or the minister and make my complaint. In these particulars we have indicated the salaries of these people. If no action is taken I wonder who would be to blame? Would it be the minister, his deputy, the acting deputy minister, or some other official of the department? If a postmaster gives unsatisfactory service or is too bold I do not hold him responsible; I hold the minister, the deputy, the acting deputy or some official at Ottawa responsible. We have to consider from what point orders come.
I have directed to one of those officials a very serious complaint. Two letters had been opened, and had been sent to Mr. Green. Two months ago they were sent to the inside service at Ottawa. The first letter was sent two months ago and the second letter about two weeks after. I received acknowledgment of the fact that the letters had been received. No action has been taken, but a week or two ago I received a letter from the minister saying that he had the matter under advisement.
There is a nigger in the wood-pile. It is not the nigger in the wood-pile who opens the letter, but it is the nigger in the wood-pile who prevents the one who opens the letter from being fired. This procedure is against regulation. It is the only case I have brought to the attention of the Post Office Department since the elections, and in this instance I made the complaint and asked that a postmaster be fired because presumably two letters had been opened by him.
An investigation has been carried on at Quebec or Ottawa, I do not know where, but I do know that I have received no satisfactory answer yet. Now here is a puzzle, Mr. Chairman. When the inside service here is responsible for allowing a postmaster to open two letters against the law of this country, how many letters can a postmaster open in over two months? That is a nice puzzle. In the meantime the public suffers, and it suffers not so much because the postmaster opened letters at a distant point from Ottawa, but because there is no sanction here. This is not a question of political partisanship at all; it is a question of fairness.

That offence is covered
by the criminal code, under the Post Office Act.

Yes. It is most unfair.
I do not ask for any prosecution against that man. I would have been satisfied in having him fired and replaced by another man for whose appointment there was a very large petition. It did not reach the outside service; it did not reach me; I do not know what is going on. The Post Office Department is a chamber of mysteries. I do not know what happens there, but it seems that everybody in that department is a frozen asset. It took me a long time to say that, but now the country must know what is going on, and it is impossible to get a satisfactory answer from the Post Office Department right now. Who is responsible for that state of affairs? Is it any one of the gentlemen whose salaries are covered by this page and a half in the estimates? I do not know, but this state of affairs cannot continue. Something must be done. I waited patiently for a very long time. I said, I will wait for better times, but better times have not come yet. Will they come in the future? I do not know. I shall have much to say about political partisanship in the future, but just now I wonder what is wrong here. Is there no grease in the wheels and axles? I have no oil can to lubricate them. I do not know what is wrong, but I would
Supply-Post Office

like to have a satisfactory answer from the minister, and to know why that postmaster who presumably has opened two letters is Still in office enjoying the benefits of the postmastership, and why the member of parliament for Temiscouata has not received a satisfactory reply to his letter of over a month and a half ago.

I did not
want to interrupt my hon. friend after he had started, but it would seem that the matter has not been attended to with any great dispatch. There is no doubt about that, and I must apologize to the member for Temiscouata, who is always so courteous, if his letter has not been answered. Really I had forgotten that I had received a letter from him that had not been answered. I assume his letter was acknowledged when I received it, and that I directed an investigation to take place. The assistant deputy tells me that a report on this matter came in to-day, and a copy of it is now on its way to my hon. friend. Perhaps when I see it and hear what has taken place I will be able to give some further explanation of why it has not been possible for me to send the report sooner.

I thank the hon. member for his explanation, but I am very much surprised at the telepathy that exists. The report has come in to-night, and I am to receive a copy of it to-night. But I am here. Why does not the minister read the answer to the committee now in order that the members may see that my complaint was fully justified? It is not a matter of being unpleasant to my friend the Postmaster General, but here we are, members of the House of Commons, and we take responsibility for what we say. This is a most serious matter. It is not a matter of making apologies. It is a matter of going straight, of going forward, of seeing that- the laws of the land shall be kept. That is as I understand it. It is not a matter of patting one on the shoulder. No, sir, it is a matter of managing a department so that everyone is treated squarely, and when a postmaster or anyone else commits an offence or does not abide by the regulations that he has to follow, of seeing that punishment comes.
I do not ask for the head of anyone, but I want everyone in my constituency to receive the letters which are addressed to them without being opened by any postmaster.
I will say more. If the postmaster in question-this was not the case-had been appointed on the recommendation of the member for Temiscouata himself, and had done a thing like that, I would have been the first

to ask the Postmaster General to discharge him at once. There should be no favouritism when a thing of that kind occurs; it is far too serious. How can one do business if one's letters are to be opened by a postmaster.
I accept the apology of the Postmaster General. When offering his apologies he did what he had to do, but it would have been much better for him if he had made no apology, if he had had no reason to make an apology. Sir, in what times do we live 1 I do not want to be hard on my hon. friend the Postmaster General, but because of the frozen assets that exist in his department, I have hundreds of letters with regard to post office matters, mail contracts and postmasters, which have been unanswered1. Why? I knew very well that I would receive no satisfactory reply and I told my people: Do not expect a satisfactory reply until such time as matters are adjusted. When anything of that kind occurs there is only one thing to do, and that is to bring the matter to the attention of the minister in charge. Then the minister should have an investigation made at the earliest possible opportunity, and then he should do the same as the League of Nations does-apply sanctions. This is a case when sanctions should be applied forthwith.
Not military sanctions.

No. Sanctions for peace,
order and good government. The minister has offered his apologies. That is very nice. It is the same as a confession of misjudgment. But I do not know who is responsible for the delay. I have no right to impute blame to anyone; I am too fair for that. Nevertheless there is a nigger in the wood-pile. Who is he? What is his name?
Put him out.

I hear hon. members say, Put him out. That is right, but how can we put him out without knowing who he is. It seems to amuse hon. gentlemen, but that is the situation. Who is the nigger? There is one page and a half in the estimates dealing with salaries paid to employees of the Post Office Department. These pages are printed in black on white, so who is the black one? Who is the black sheep? Will the minister be kind enough to tell me who is responsible for this matter being held up for such a long time? Why is it that on this day, March 23,
I have learned only ten minutes ago that a reply is in my box down in the post office.

No; it has not reached me yet.

Supply-Post Office

My hon. friend just said that it was on the way to me, and it has not yet reached him. The Post Office Department seems to be a chamber of mysteries. It would provide fine material for a detective novel.
Let us be serious. I have every sympathy for the Postmaster General and he knows this is the first time I have raised my voice in connection with what has been going on in his department since the election. I do not complain very often. I took my time and I waited to give other hon. members an opportunity to settle their cases. But nothing has been done and I have waited a long time. It is pitiful to have to write to constituents who are asking what action has been taken:
Dear Sir:
I regret very much to tell you that no action has been taken because it would appear that the Postmaster General is unwilling to take any. Therefore, I cannot give you a definite answer. Perhaps things will be easier in the near or distant future, but at present I do not know.
There is nothing more unsatisfactory than to say, "I do not know." No one seems to know about this matter; it is a complete mystery. I have a very high regard for the officials of this department. They are able men with a high sense of duty. The same can be said of the Department of Labour. Some of the officials in that department appeared to be incompetent last year, but that was because the minister was preventing them from showing their real ability. With a new minister at the head of the department the situation is entirely different. There are men in the Post Office Department who were there when the Hon. Mr. Murphy was Postmaster General; they were there under the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot); they were there under the Hon. Mr. Sauve. They seem to be frozen assets and I do not know that I blame them for that as they work in a frigid atmosphere. There is something wrong in the department. I have the highest regard for these officials and I think they should be left free to do their duty. This is entirely different from a question of political partisanship; it concerns administration and management. Why should we not receive more satisfactory treatment? I cannot understand it, and no one can understand it. Will the minister kindly tell the committee who is responsible for holding up this matter for such a long time?

I can speak for only a few moments. I may say to my
hon. friend that his mention of this matter was the first I learned of it since I received his letter some time ago. If he wrote me that letter two months ago and he has not received a reply, I really cannot tell him now why a reply has not been sent. I want to say to him that he has been more considerate of my time than other hon. gentlemen who have had similar matters to bring before the department; they generally bring them up at least once every two weeks. It is not that I have not been writing letters because I spend a good deal of my time answering various people. I have not answered my hon. friend because I have not had the report. I am sure he will be satisfied when I show him the report and give him the explanation. Perhaps matters might have been checked up a little more, but apparently this has not been attended to.
I take it that the postmaster is found guilty?

I am not going to pass judgment on anyone until I see the report. When judgment is passed I hope it will be satisfactory to everyone concerned.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, March 24, 1936
